other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "elmerjfudd", "author_name": "Elmer J Fudd", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/elmerjfudd", "date": "2023-01-02", "text": "I suggest you NOT seal and close the opening. In my area, when a gas burning appliance is in a closed interior closet, the building code requires two holes that reach outside air- one in or near the ceiling (so that a leak of lighter than air natural gas can escape) and one in or at the floor, for combustion air for the appliance to use. We are experiencing gaps between boards in our newly installed 3/4\" oak flooring.  Gaps in crown moulding joints are appearing.  Doors are beginning to catch/drag at the corners. What is the optimum humidity level for a house?  The standard is apparently 70 F and 50% humidity.  It seems like a whole house humidification and dehumidification system may be needed to maintain the humidity at a constant level. title: 600 cfm ventahood sufficient for wok cooking? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "martin-yang61", "author_name": "Martin Yang", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/martin-yang61", "date": "2023-01-02", "text": "Recently I installed a 36 inch capital culinarian and a 42 inch 600 cfm ventahood magic lung for my kitchen to do some high heat cooking. Unfortunately it seems the suction is insufficient. Here you see the smoke going straight up when seasoning the wok. https://streamable.com/c1hzocThe appliance installer insisted 6 inch round is sufficient even though the installation manual specified 8 inch round. The roof vent is also a square low profile box vent. Do you guys think changing tubing to an 8 inch round and the roof vent to a gooseneck vent would make this good enough or do I need to get the 900 or 1200 cfm vent for my needs.From what I've been reading 600 cfm should have been more than sufficient?TIA", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kaseki", "author_name": "kaseki", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kaseki", "date": "2023-01-02", "text": "It's hard to determine scale from that image, but generally rectangular sections with one dimension relatively narrow have small equivalent round duct capacity. Magic Lung hoods avoid the pressure loss of baffles, but the blower(s) used are fairly sensitive to duct restrictions, AND MAKE-UP AIR RESTRICTIONS.  You didn't describe your MUA system. I would put a proper roof cap into place -- which you seem to be in process of doing, increase the duct size to 8 or 10 inches, upgrade the hood to dual 600 CFM blowers, and ensure that the make-up air system provides interior pressure that is within a tenth of an inch water column to the pressure outside.  Note that using undersized duct relative to the instructions should have been flagged by the building code inspector. It is worth pointing out yet again that hoods only capture plume effluent if it more or less naturally rises into the hood entry aperture.  Hoods do not suction from the cooktop, or from points a few inches away from the hood skirt, as your video aptly demonstrates.  Ideally, your hood should overlap the pan/wok boundary by about 6 inches. For the observant: When you pass your favorite Asian food restaurant, try to observe the roof.  On it you will see one or more up-blast commercial blowers, and also at least one device that looks like a rectangular box with an angled screen at one end.  This latter assembly is the MUA system for the restaurant, and it has to provide exactly the same amount of air flow rate (CFM) as the exhaust blowers are removing from the kitchen space.", "images": []}}

Corresponding CFM can be calculated from the apparent area, although in most cases I've seen, the area equivalent is itself over-valuing the non-linear effects of a multiplicity of small apertures. In any case, most down-draft assemblies are sold as part of a system that includes a blower that the manufacturer believes is suitable.  Such blowers may be designed for higher pressure loss.  I haven't investigated this topic in detail because downdraft schemes are functionally the wrong approach. If you want to do-it-yourself, you will need to evaluate the pressure loss vs. flow rate of the aperture assembly, throw in some more for ducting and imperfect make-up air, and hunt through the fan curves of candidate blowers to find a suitable blower. At best the pop-up type can deviate low momentum steam plumes, so maybe plumes from simmering bacon or poaching fish on a back burner can be partly captured. title: New Kitchen Vent DOESN'T suck | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-432356109", "author_name": "HU-432356109", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-432356109", "date": "2023-01-03", "text": "Hello Everyone, We just moved into a new house where the kitchen vent above the gas stove (NuTone) is new, but it doesn't suck in the kitchen vapors/fumes. The filters of the vent are new, as is the fan inside, no grease, rattling, or obstructions, and everything from the outside (fan/lights) works perfectly. When trying to hold a sheet of paper to the vent filters, one area on the two filters seems to attract the sheet more than the other. Our guess is that the flexi-pipes right above the unit (inside a cabinet), or all the way in the attic have either a kink, or may have been misaligned. Like a very expensive vacuum cleaner with a flexible tube that is not sealed all the way, or has a tiny hole. Has anyone ever had such a problem? How did you troubleshoot and fix it? Thanks for all the helpful replies. EDIT: Did some research and the unit resembles a NuTone Mantra AVSF1. EDIT 2: The house itself is not new, only all of the kitchen appliances are.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kaseki", "author_name": "kaseki", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kaseki", "date": "2023-01-03", "text": "\"...375 Max Blower CFM-rated hood...\"  Actual flow likely only 200 CFM with correct ducting and lossless MUA.  Rated means blower operating hanging in free air without any pressure losses, particularly those of the mesh filters. Only fume hoods used for grinding and welding develop enough flow (and noise) to suck vapors to them for removal; cooking ventilation that anyone could stand depends on the hood's capture area intercepting the rising and expanding cooking plumes.  In canopy hoods, that is the boundary area at the bottom.  On this decorative hood, it might be the mesh areas.  These are not overlapping the potential cooking plumes that the cooktop below can generate, depending on pan sizes, and no means of retaining plume components that reflect from the sheet metal are present. Likely the installer was depending on house leakage for MUA.  This requires a pressure drop between outside and inside, and this drop reduces blower performance. At a minimum, the installation instructions should be reviewed to determine correct ducting.", "images": []}}

title: Setting an IntelliFlo VF pump on "timed manual" mode??? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "nick-shirley", "author_name": "nick_shirley", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/nick-shirley", "date": "2023-01-03", "text": "I have an IntelliFlo VF pump that has worked perfectly for my 19,500 gal. pool since the pump was installed in 2009.  Shortly after install, I started using Manual mode rather than either Filter or Feature modes because it gave me complete control over flow rate and energy usage, rather than depending on the computer in the pump to decide what's best for me.  I've run it 24 hours a day at about 1,550, which pulls about 204 - 230 watts depending on filter cleanliness.  I've been happy with these settings, never having any sort of algae or cloudiness issue despite keeping the chlorine levels on the low side, despite living in Palm Springs where 122 degree highs in the summer are not unknown, and despite having water temps in the very high nineties in July, August, and early September.  Accordingly, I'm just fine with the pool circulation 24 hours a day at that flow rate. Recently my electrical company put me into a new plan where the KwH price doubles between 4pm and 9pm each and every day of the week.  The obvious response is to have the pump shut off during those hours while upping the RPMs a bit for the remaining 20 hours in order to compensate for the reducing run times. This idea of removing the tub and reusing the floor tile to fill in where the tub had been has a major flaw.  No waterproofing.  Your plan only takes into account the pretty surfaces and not the bones that actually make a shower work.  When you build a shower, the layers underneath the tile and grout must be waterproof.  Grout is not waterproof.  A shower is built to account for that and you can actually take a shower in a properly made shower BEFORE the tile and grout go in and you will be fine.  If you leave up walls from the 1950s or earlier, you are dealing with tile set into a thick mud base reinforced with wire mesh.  Somehow, this system usually did not leak through and get the framing of the walls wet.  But once the tub is gone, you are back to bare studs down there. Your new section where the tub had been will either just leak, will leak at the seam between the old wall and the new area of wall (if you manage to waterproof the new section), or will leak both where this seam is and where the new wall meets the shower floor.  The only way to make a waterproof shower is to have a seamless layer of waterproofing using one of several methods from the drain in the shower floor to the top of the tile walls AFTER a professional slopes the shower floor properly.  You simply cannot do it the way that you said you want to do it, re-using the floor tiles to make the lower walls. main_question: {"author_id": "gsciencechick", "author_name": "gsciencechick", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gsciencechick", "date": "2023-01-03", "text": "Hi, everyone, we just found out little girl kitty (the one in my profile photo) is now hyperthyroid. I am not surprised because the past couple months she has been out of control with wanting food, and she has lost a little bit of weight even though she is tiny already. We had a hyperthyroid cat before and gave him methimazole, and had regular bloodwork. This was not easy because he was not good with taking pills. So, we want to look into the radioactive treatment since it is available in our area. She is 13. All her other bloodwork is good, but I have to try to get a urine sample. From what I've read, she will need to be there about 4 days, we can't visit,  and then afterwards needs to have limited contact with us and also the other cat. For example, cannot sit in lap and cannot sleep with us or I guess him.   How have you handled this isolation?  We have a very small house, so we would probably use the guest room since I use the computer room for work. So, if you have any experience, I'd like to hear from you.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "anniedeighnaugh", "author_name": "Annie Deighnaugh", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/anniedeighnaugh", "date": "2023-01-04", "text": "I would strongly recommend against it.  Instead ask about treating first with methimazole.  Meds can be adjusted for the needs of the cat, but radiation cannot and is permanent.  It results in the permanent destruction of an essential body organ.  A friend chose radiation instead and his cat died.  The radiation treatment can lead to thyroid storm which can be fatal. The reason I feel so strongly about this is because I was hyperthyroid and I too chose medication.  I was able to wean off the medication after several months and was back to normal.  This happened with our cat as well where he was able to be normal without medication after some time. Look at it this way...if the meds don't work, you can stop the pills and still do the radiation. title: Austausch der Fensterverglasung | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-500781096", "author_name": "Chris Kai", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-500781096", "date": "2023-01-04", "text": "Hallo Community,Ich ben\u00f6tige bitte Eure Unterst\u00fctzung in meinem Brainstorming. Im April zogen wir in ein Haus aus der Ende der 80er Jahre. An sich ist es sehr solide und hochwertig gebaut worden. Problematisch erweisen sich derzeit die Fenster. Einige von denen w\u00fcrde ich aus Sicherheitsgr\u00fcnden austauschen und auch Rollos einbauen und manche w\u00fcrde ich gerne belassen. Die Fenster sind aus Holz, super Zustand, nur die Verglasung scheint doppelt, aber ohne das Gas in der Mitte zu sein. Ich habe gelesen, dass es m\u00f6glich w\u00e4re in die alten Fenster eine neue Doppelverglasung mit Gas dazwischen einzubauen. Wer macht denn so was? Ich finde nicht viel dazu im Internet. Macht es preislich einen Unterschied, im Vergleich zum Komplettaustausch? Da ich im ganzen Haus sehr ungew\u00f6hnliche und keine zwei gleichen Fenster habe, w\u00e4re es mir lieber die sehr sch\u00f6nen Holzfenster \u00fcberwiegend zu belassen und nur etwas auf den neueren Stand (nicht neusten, da nur 2fach Verglasung) zu bringen. Was h\u00e4lt ihr davon?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~689457039", "author_name": "Raumagentur ArteFakt", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~689457039", "date": "2023-01-11", "text": "Meinung und Wissen kommen in Foren leider nicht immer \u00fcberein.Das Glas ist bei Holzfenstern in der Tat die gr\u00f6\u00dfere Schwachstelle. Und auch Gasgef\u00fcllte Doppelverglasung verliert im Laufe der Zeit das Gas, was zu einem erh\u00f6hten W\u00e4rmedurchgang f\u00fchrt. Die Rahmen aus Holz sind dagegen kaum verlustbehaftet, und auch kaum ver\u00e4ndert in den letzten Jahren, ganz im Gegensatz zu Kunststoff- oder Metallrahmen, die mittlerweile f\u00fcr bessere D\u00e4mmwerte aus mehr Kammern bestehen als damals. Wenn ein Einsatz von 3fach-Verglasung sowieso aus technischen Gr\u00fcnden entf\u00e4llt, haben die Fl\u00fcgeltahmen nicht einmal ein entscheidend h\u00f6heres Gewicht zu tragen.Und man sollte alle Parameter betrachten. Ein Glastausch verbessert den D\u00e4mmwert, ohne da\u00df die Laibungen im Mauerwerk oder die Fensterb\u00e4nke nachgearbeitet oder gar ersetzt werden m\u00fcssen. Ein Faktor, der durch die Arbeit verschiedener Gewerke keine zu vernachl\u00e4ssigende finanzielle Gr\u00f6\u00dfe ist. Die Differenz vom Glasaustausch zu neuem Komplettfenster mag in Relation gering sein (bei Kunststofffenstern geringer als bei Holzfenstern), doch in Summe und unter Ber\u00fccksichtigung notwendiger zus\u00e4tzlicher Nacharbeiten durchaus entscheidend.Au\u00dferdem ist es nichts verkehrt die Nachhaltigkeit in die \u00dcberlegungen mit einzubeziehen. In der Regel ist ein Fensterrahmen ein Block, der innen gef\u00e4lzt ist. In diese Falz wird das Glas gestellt, und durch eine innenliegende Glashalteleiste umlaufend fixiert. Diese Glashalteleiste kann recht einfach entfernt werden, und eine neue Doppelverglasung eingebracht werden. Je nach Ausf\u00fchrungstiefe der Falz kann man durch Verwendung einer schlankeren Glashalteleiste sogar eine dickere Scheibe mit einer besseren Gasschicht einsetzen. Die einzige H\u00fcrde ist, jemanden zu finden, der den Austausch vornimmt. Inkl. Ausbau, Messen, bestellen, neu vergossen und ggfls. neuen Halteleisten. Ein Fensterbauer ist da oft NICHT der Ansprechpartner, weil das h\u00e4ufig Fensterh\u00e4ndler sind, mit einem Montageteam. Ein Schreiner mit eigener Werkstatt ist hier sicher zielf\u00fchrender.", "images": []}}

title: Cool ERV Exhaust blown directly on Heat pump coil increase Efficency? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jason-moss69", "author_name": "Jason Moss", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jason-moss69", "date": "2023-01-06", "text": "I am building a house that has several heat pumps in Southern Arizona. My question is if I route the cool exhaust from my ERV system to blow directly onto my outdoor heat pump coil, would that increase the AC/heat pumps Efficiency? If the heat pumps job is extract cool air would that not make its job a little easier???", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/c012b62603b7e060_4916-w500-h272-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~1291890641", "author_name": "Charles Ross Homes", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~1291890641", "date": "2023-01-19", "text": "I understand the proposed configuration.  The potential energy savings at the condenser is equal to the amount of energy which the ERV failed to transfer. So you can do a back-of-the-envelope estimate if you know the temperature conditions and the efficiency of the ERV.  Assuming an ERV efficiency of 80% that leaves a potential 20% that could possibly be recouped under ideal conditions.  However, doing so will require more energy to deliver the ERV exhaust to the condenser, and keeping the exhaust point close enough to the condenser to capture the benefit will interfere with the flow of regular outdoor air.   My back-of-the-envelope calc suggests a 2.5% potential on a 98F day; less at lower temps.  It's a classic case of diminishing returns.", "images": []}}

title: Tips for Quick House Cleaning | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "wallpaper-as-a-lifestyle-pfvwgb-pf~1799972154", "author_name": "Wallpaper as a lifestyle", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/interior-designers-and-decorators/wallpaper-as-a-lifestyle-pfvwgb-pf~1799972154", "date": "2023-01-06", "text": "It's that time of year again. The holidays are almost at their end, which comes with an inescapable share of cleaning across several households worldwide. This situation comes with the need to clean the house quickly yet effectively. While some are familiar with these processes, others require tips on how to do them.Understanding housekeeping tips can enable you to complete tasks more quickly and maintain a spotless home with little hassle. This post will help you understand tips for keeping your home clean this holiday. Join us as we take you through them.1. Take a rubbish walk around your houseIt is easier to determine how much tidying your house requires than to take a cautious stroll through it. So, when you start walking around, make sure you have a plastic bag with you. This way, if you come across any rubbish or other junk you need to throw out, you can pick it up, put it in the bag, and get rid of a lot while exploring the rest of your home.When you take the time to gather this information now, you can prevent it from consuming additional time in the future.Before the primary cleaning, you should also finish any necessary dishes. The worktops in your kitchen should be convenient for cleaning because you don't want to move any plates in the middle of the process.2. Prepare your cleaning suppliesYour cleaning supplies are the catalysts you need to speed up this cleaning process. So to avoid returning to your cabinets to get more items, collect them all together and carry them with you as you move from room to room.Your toolbox ought to contain clean-up clothes, a laundry basket, a rubbish bag, and a carpet cleaner, to mention a few. You can pack them together in a caddy, bucket, or tote. This will make cleaning much more straightforward because everything you require is in one mobile location.You should ensure that your vacuum is with you. This way, you can give the carpets a quick once-over when you've finished cleaning the rest of the room.Also, feel free to add the necessary materials for your residence. eMop ensures that they use material tailored to your house's needs. For instance, you can include some wax or polish if your flooring is wooden.3. Begin at the room's ceilingIt's natural to want to vacuum dirty carpets the moment you see them. Avoid giving in to that need and start at the bottom of the room.This might be the shelves, the counters, the cabinets' tops, or the room's corners. When you do this first, you will have time to vacuum up any dust that may fall from the shelves or other surfaces.Beginning at the bottom increases the chance that your floor will be messier and dustier than when you started. So please don't do it because it negates the whole purpose of cleaning.4. Gather ClustersExamine the items accumulated in each room as you move from one to the next. Take them back to their proper place if they don't belong here. You can do this room by room. If you find something out of place in a room, gather it in a bag or your laundry basket, then put it back after you're finished with the room.Even if something belongs in space, ask yourself if you could arrange it more neatly. Then, be it magazines, appliances, or even worn-out sneakers, you should factor in storing, disposing or donating every item as you gather them.You can even get creative with how and where you collect these clusters.5. Consider using a Feather DusterMany associate feather dusters with cleaning objects belonging to a bygone age. But they need to learn that they are incredibly beneficial for cleaning their homes. They can fit into small spaces much more quickly than you can with a cloth and your hand. An excellent example is cleaning window curtains or the tiniest crevices on shelves.They could be more effective at eliminating significant volumes of dust. Still, if your house is dusty, they can make a substantial change.6. Clean up your kitchenYour kitchen will inevitably become oily. Grease can still adhere to the shelves above or the sides of your stove even if you wipe it after every usage.When this occurs, you should use a liquid detergent similar to what you would use in your dishwasher. You can also mix vinegar with water to create a disinfectant that is safe.Given that some of these mixtures can harm wood and paintings, you should try this on a specific area hidden from sight.7. Focus on the bathrooms, sinks, and toiletsSpray cleaning solution over the kitchen sink before cleaning the bathroom sinks, tubs, and toilets. Let it settle for a bit so that there's time to get rid of the dirt and stains. Afterward, return to the kitchen and start cleaning. Don't forget to wipe the inside of the microwave. Tidying bathrooms comes at the end.", "images": []}

title: Contractor painter vs independent? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "evelynsmom", "author_name": "evelynsmom", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/evelynsmom", "date": "2023-01-06", "text": "Question is, should I have my contractors do the painting, or hire someone independently?  (I can do a change order if I choose to use someone else.) Context: I'm in the middle of a major renovation with a contractor.  We've had a lot of serious issues with them, so that I feel I'm project managing, despite not being handy and having never done another renovation before.   Here are just a few: I believe there are advantages to having your contractor take responsibility for the paint because they get a good contractor discount for the paint, any defects would be covered by the 2-year warranty we get with the overall home (although I believe there are many, many exclusions). However, I also think that if I were to hire someone independent, they may spot defects in the drywall/taping/trim, etc. that I may not spot on my own. The independent person I'm thinking of is my handyman who cleans my eavestroughs and also has done a small exterior painting job (very well) for me a few years ago.  He also does eavestroughs and other handyman work for many of the homes in our neighbourhood so I know he will always be around if I had any problems and wanted him to touch up something down the road.  And I would have to supply the paint, but then I'd at least have confidence it's the paint I asked for. On the \"cons\" side, he's just one guy, so may make slower progress than whatever team our contractor would use, especially if he feels the trim isn't in good shape and that the millwork needs caulking/sanding, etc. before he can proceed.  I worry about this part because I feel the contractor may dig in their heels about cooperating with our painter if he feels the millwork isn't in good enough shape and they disagree and say some of that is our painter's responsibility and/or that they think it is good enough. I am using independent folks to do my carpet (totally trust him since he did our basement carpet 12 years ago), kitchen installation (since our contractors don't do kitchen installation) and marmoleum kitchen floor (since our contractors don't have experience with Marmoleum).  Each of these is a bit more complicated because I have to be the go-between between the contractor and independent supplier. These are just the pros and cons I can think of.  There are likely many more I haven't thought of. What do you all think of whether I should proceed with my contractor for painting vs. not?", "images": []}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "bry911", "author_name": "bry911", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bry911", "date": "2023-01-06", "text": "So first, you can't buy sold wood doors for what you can make them for. main_question: {"author_id": "stm25rs", "author_name": "stm25rs", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/stm25rs", "date": "2023-01-06", "text": "I'm doing a new construction home build, and looking at water heaters. Will be ~2500 sq ft finished space, 3 bed, 3 full bath. It will just be my fianc\u00e9e and I living there, and no kids in our future, but will have friends and family staying with us for long weekends. The master shower will have his and her shower heads each having an angled sprayer and a handheld on a rail slider, and a soaking tub, probably ~65 gallons. We were initially thinking whole home electric tankless, but the more I read about those, the less interested I am. I've essentially ruled them out unless I'm missing a good reason to use them, and we aren't interested in doing a propane tank with a propane tankless heater. There's no natural gas service in the neighborhood. Project is near Baltimore, MD, climate zone 7b, on municipal water service. I'm currently thinking a hybrid water heater, but we need to size for sufficient hot water for when we have guests, and to fill the soaking tub, which would likely mean an 80 gallon tank. But we also don't want to constantly heat an 80 gallon tank if possible. I see there's this Rheem booster, which appear to just be a 7kW electric tankless heater designed for horizontal install, with horizontal display. Does this sound like a good fit for our needs? Or is there another alternative solution to consider?", "images": []}

It had a triple-whammy of stressors starting just over a year ago, and I haven't been able to recover it. 1) I moved twice in four months, and the first location had very poor natural light. It went from a room where it had 2 - 5 hours of direct morning sun to basically no natural sunlight. The second place (my current apartment) has great light, so I don't think that's the current problem. 2) Over the next few months after the move, older leaves started turning yellow and falling off. The plant had only lost 3 leaves the entire life of the plant up to that point, and then one was dying every other week or so. I thought maybe it had outgrown the pot (it was almost entirely root; there wasn't really any way to change the soil because it was all root ball), so I re-potted it. The new pot is about 1.5x larger. Obviously monsteras don't like to be moved around, but I didn't think there was another option. 3) There was / is something wrong with the new potting soil I used. After watering it the normal amount that I had in the old pot, I noticed that the soil wasn't draining despite the pot having a separate tray and a layer of crushed rock at the bottom to keep the roots off the floor. I stopped watering the plant but didn't do anything else (didn't change the soil which I probably should have. Too late now though). The leaves kept dying, and then the worst part: the roots and stem sections that were in the soil had COMPLETELY rotted. Everything below the dirt level is black and shriveled. Miraculously, the plant is still alive. I planted an arial root in a small pot I nailed to the wall (lol), and that root is growing super quickly into the soil. Other than that, I have no idea how it's getting enough nutrients to sustain itself. The soil is finally dry. The leaves are curling under and some of them have brown tips, but given the state of the roots I'm honestly shocked it's not worse or already dead. So here's my question: what should I do? I've seen suggestions that involve taking the plant out of the pot, cleaning all the roots off and re-potting. Not sure about this strategy given that a) all the roots appear dead already anyway and b) it was stressful enough the first time I moved it around. Also what's weird about the soil is I potted a weeping fig with the exact same dirt from the same bag and it's totally fine. No weird draining issues and the plant looks really happy and is shooting out new leaves like nobody's business. So I have no idea what happened there. Anyway, would love advice here! other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "frank-laudone", "author_name": "frank_laudone", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/frank-laudone", "date": "2023-01-07", "text": "", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/7072d8d103b998ce_7670-w240-h426-b0-p0--.jpg"]}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "socks12345", "author_name": "socks", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/socks12345", "date": "2023-01-08", "text": "I think it looks fine.", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2023-01-14", "text": "Choosing an Appropriate Size Container How large a container \u2018can\u2019 or \u2018should\u2019 be, depends on the relationship between the mass of the plant material you are working with and your choice of grow media. We often concern ourselves with \"over-potting\" (using a container that is too large), but \"over-potting\" is a term that arises from a lack of a basic understanding about the relationship we will look at, which logically determines appropriate container size. It's often repeated that you should only move up one container size when \"potting-up\". The reasoning is, that when potting up to a container more than one size larger, the medium will remain wet too long and potentially cause root rot issues, or at a minimum, limited root function. In reality, it is the size/mass of the plant material you are working with, and the physical properties of the medium you choose that determines both the upper & lower limits of appropriate container size - not a formulaic upward progression of container sizes. In many cases, after root pruning a plant, it may even be appropriate to step down a container size or two, but as you will see, that also depends on the physical properties of the medium you choose. It's not uncommon for me, after a repot/root-pruning to pot in containers as small as 1/5 the size as that which the plant had been growing in prior to the work. Plants grown in \u2018slow\u2019 (slow-draining/water-retentive) media need to be grown in containers with smaller volumes so the plant can use water quickly, allowing air to return to the medium before root issues more serious than impaired root function/metabolism become a limiting factor. We know that the anaerobic (airless) conditions that accompany soggy media quickly kill fine roots and impair root function/metabolism. We also know smaller medium volumes and the root constriction that accompany them cause plants to both extend branches and gain o/a mass much more slowly - a bane if rapid growth is the goal - a boon if growth restriction and a compact plant are what you have your sights set on. Conversely, rampant growth can be had by growing in very large containers and in very fast (draining) media where frequent watering and fertilizing is required - so it's not that plants rebel at being potted into very large containers per se, but rather, they rebel at being potted into very large containers in a medium too slow and water-retentive. This is a key point. We know there is an inverse relationship between media particle size and the height of the perched water table (PWT) in containers. A PWT is water that fills spaces between soil particles and defies gravity by refusing to leave the pot. As particle size increases, the height of the PWT decreases, until at about a particle size of just under 1/8 inch, media will no longer hold perched water. If there is no perched water, the medium is ALWAYS well aerated, even when it is at container capacity (fully saturated). So, if you aim for a medium (like the gritty mix) composed primarily of particles larger than 1/16\", there is no upper limit to container size, other than what you can practically manage. The lower size limit will be determined by the medium volume's ability to allow room for roots to \u2019run\u2019 and to furnish water enough to sustain the plant between irrigations. Bearing heavily on this ability is the ratio of fine roots to coarse roots. It takes a minimum amount of fine rootage to support the canopy under high water demand. If the container is full of large roots, there may not be room for a sufficient volume of the fine roots that do all the water/nutrient delivery work, and the coarse roots, too. You can grow a very large plant in a very small container if the roots have been well managed and the lion's share of the rootage is fine. You can also grow very small plants, even seedlings, in seemingly inordinately large containers if the medium is fast (free-draining and well-aerated) enough that it holds no, or very little perched water. I have just offered clear illustration why the oft repeated advice to \u2018resist potting up more than one pot size at a time\u2019, only applies when using heavy, water-retentive media. Well-aerated media are not bound by the same restrictions. As the ht and volume of the perched water table are reduced, the potential for negative effects associated with over-potting are diminished in a direct relationship with the reduction - up to the point at which the soil holds no (or an insignificant amount) of perched water and over-potting pretty much becomes a non-issue. title: Life in January | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2023-01-08", "text": "January for many is a thankless month, and ours has been more thankless than usual.  After Christmas we all caught Covid and spent some days limp, blanketed, and huddled around the wood stove, getting up only to feed ourselves or the fire.  Currently we're convalescent.  The weather has continued as it's been since November, I think:  cloudy, foggy, but largely rainless; dark, dark, dark. Of course, compared with many, we're fortunate.  We have enough money to heat and eat; the weather is dull as all get out, but isn't bringing natural disasters. title: help finding right organic sweet Corn seeds in Canada | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "doriswk", "author_name": "doriswk", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/doriswk", "date": "2023-01-08", "text": "I am in zone 5, Toronto, Canada, and am looking for organic non GMO sweet corn seeds for corn that has ca 8\" long ears, grows at least 6' tall,  and from which I can collect seeds for planting in the following year. Last year I planted \"Early Sunglow\" sweet corn which produced  short stalks and short (max 6\") cobs which my husband did not enjoy. Further, I had planted beans to climb up the stalks ( the 3 sisters method), and the beans did not appreciate the short stalks at all, had to supplement with stakes. .. Searching for organic non GMO sweet corn seeds online seems to bring up varieties for short growing seasons with short stalks and short ears. I did find 2 Canadian suppliers selling organic non GMO Peaches and Cream Corn and Serendipity corn seeds, both regular size, but these are hybrid seeds.   Has anyone collected seeds from these and planted successfully? I read that if collecting seeds from hybrid corn, the new plants grown from these seeds will not be true, may revert back to original plant. I wonder, do people keep buying corn seeds, or are there non hybrid  varieties available suitable for seed collecting ? Many US suppliers wont ship to Canada.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "daninthedirt", "author_name": "daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/daninthedirt", "date": "2023-01-10", "text": "Very simply, hybrids that produce desirable plants may come from crossed plants that are individually not so desirable. main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-159822510", "author_name": "R E", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-159822510", "date": "2023-01-08", "text": "Hi, I\u2019m new to this forum, but expect I\u2019ll be posting a fair bit over the coming months as I start tackling work in my recently purchased bungalow. Background: It\u2019s a fairly typical 60s bungalow. I\u2019ve recently had contractors in to remove the (asbestos containing) Artex ceilings, as well as Asbestos tiling that was covering the floors in the bedrooms. It\u2019s this that I\u2019m now considering doing follow-up work on. Having lifted the tiles, it appears that they were glued down using bitumen. I had this tested for Asbestos (in a different area of the property) and this came back negative, so I\u2019m assuming that\u2019s the case all the way through. I also understand that this bitumen would have acted as a rudimentary DPM. My issues now are two fold. Firstly, there are now holes in the bitumen, both from where some bright spark had nailed gripper rod into the Asbestos tiles and concrete beneath, as well as the odd hole that looks like may have been historic wiring: https://imgur.com/a7TMh5i You can also see that the bitumen doesn\u2019t run right to the edges. I\u2019m a bit concerned that these may compromise the surface, and I\u2019m not sure if the concrete beneath has a proper DPM below this. I\u2019m doubly concerned because my property is in an area that\u2019s at moderate risk of groundwater flooding. At the same time, the floors are not level. So I\u2019m considering the best option for fixing the floors - I may be worrying about nothing, but I\u2019d like to get things done right once, and not have to worry about them again, and would like to get back to level floors that will be water resistant. From my reading online, it looks like one option may be an Ardex DPM sandwich - a layer of their SLC (which I understand binds ok to Bitumen), a DPM then another SLC layer. Does anyone have any experience with this in situations like mine, or have any other suggestions? Also, this is a basic question, but what contractor should I get out to carry out these works? Would this just be a regular builder, or would a specialist be more appropriate?", "images": []}

Your \"forcing\" the grass. I'd suggest if you want a lawn there to get a quality grass seed mix that's not from a big box store. You don't want to buy grass seed that will grow anywhere in the world. You want all the seed to be great in your area. Google Pennington seed and look for a dealer in your town. Fescues are the grass that grow well in the shade. But no one ever points out that they also don't do well in drought conditions. So they won't do well if the shade is from a huge shade tree. You want a mix with perennial rye, a fine fescue and also Kentucky Blue Grass seed in the mix. If you have all fescues or Blue Grass or only one of them you'll have to dethatch your lawn which is a big job. Also those two varieties tend to get Red Thread and Red Dust when the humidity is high in mid summer. With the mix of all three you eliminate both problems. I spread the seed by hand. Making sure I get an even spread. Take a big handful and throw it. You can only see the big rye grass seed so you'll have a lot more coverage than what you see. Be careful around garden beds to not get seed in them which you'll have to weed out. I'd suggest you cover the seed with an inch of \"mushroom compost\" which may be sold in bulk by the seed dealer. Some sellers will let you fill big contractor trash bags which you can put in your vehicle. Otherwise it's sold by the cubic yard. You could also cover the seed with peat but that tends to float away if there's any water flow thru the lawn. Using the mushroom compost will improve your soil and give you a good start to over fertilizing you shady spot. Anything less and germination will be low, the resulting grass will be sparse and weeds and moss - far more shade tolerant - will proliferate, choking out or overwhelming the struggling turf grass. There is also the issue of lack of soil moisture, root competition and soil compaction. I agree that a low growing groundcover will be your best bet. There are varieties that will be very shade and drought tolerant and most are able to support light foot traffic at the very least.  Evergreen is best :-)  Unless you prefer, it does not have to be a native species. Just make sure it will tolerate your growing conditions and is not considered an invasive species in your area.", "images": []}}

title: Bathtub waste and overflow - code? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "14belsize", "author_name": "Bongo", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/14belsize", "date": "2023-01-10", "text": "Hi, question for plumbers. We are building a new home in Nassau County, New York. The bathtub was just installed on the 2nd floor. The plumber installed Gerber brass waste & overflow in the area without future access. Bathtub sits above another half bathroom, which will be fully drywalled without future access to bathtub waste and overflow. You can\u2019t really see Gerber W & O in the picture as it\u2019s above that P trap.There is a TJI beam on the way so the plumber had to a lot of maneuvering. He tried to install Cable Operated Tub Waste and Overflow but it didn\u2019t fit because the TJI was on the way. He wanted to cut TJI and we said no. I think the cable operated unit was glue joints as it was plastic.  Does anyone know if the code requires PVC waste and overflow? Would that be NY or local or some other code? Can anyone point me in the right direction where I can find the language for the Code so I can discuss with the plumber?  It was already installed but the space below was not drywalled yet. Should we replace it now while we still have the chance?  Where would I have an access panel? There is half bathroom below bathtub and it would look really weird if we have access panel in the ceiling. I had never seen one done it this way. thank you!", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/a782122903bd5cf4_4489-w500-h317-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/ae02193203bd5cf6_4489-w500-h567-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "14belsize", "author_name": "Bongo", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/14belsize", "date": "2023-01-10", "text": "I just thought the code required glued connections (PVC?) if it was installed in inaccessible place?", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "bry911", "author_name": "bry911", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bry911", "date": "2023-01-10", "text": "My 2 cents... this is one of those be careful what you wish for situations. So, a disclaimer, my plumbing license expired 30 years ago (mostly because I stayed in college long enough to ensure I would not have to work for my father).  I am also not really familiar with New York plumbing codes but understand they can be quite a bit more strict than others.  If you want an answer from a plumber familiar with New York, then I suggest the TerryLove forums. In my limited and distant experience, the access panel requirement is overly broad and even where required is often written in pencil.  We were told to pull the tub, mount the waste and overflow and then set the tub.  Sometimes pulling the tub is impractical and so a slip joint waste and overflow is used.  Your waste and overflow are unlikely to leak over time, there just isn't any force to pull them apart, after a couple of years you could likely go cut the compression nuts off and they still wouldn't leak if you didn't disturb the pipes.  The trap itself is a different story as gravity and water are pulling it apart so I would want it to be solvent, as yours is. I personally wouldn't turn this into a problem, but if you want to be sure head over to the TerryLove forums.", "images": []}}

title: My Southwestern “Petroglyph” Fireplace | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "lynnnm", "author_name": "LynnNM", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/lynnnm", "date": "2023-01-11", "text": "OutsidePlaying asked me to explain my painted kiva fireplace, and I didn\u2019t want to take over the original thread to do it. First of all, this is a kiva (KEY-vah) fireplace, which is very common here New Mexico. They were first used in the sacred underground chambers of the Pueblo Indians as far back as the 8th century,  or before. Three of our four fireplaces are kivas. This one is in our family room and one day I just got inspired to paint something on it, as I wanted it to make a statement. I did everything except the bottom animals  just using various sized sponges. Obviously, I painted the top to represent smoke. On the base, I painted figures, like the ancient petroglyphs found many places here in NM. Petroglyphs are carvings on rocks. Many were made by the prehistoric people living here long ago and weren\u2019t made for aesthetic purposes, but were sacred images to record, warn, or teach.  So, I painted mine to represent wildlife here in New Mexico: buffalo, elk, jackrabbit,  lizard, etc. Over the years since then, our Western furniture, antiques and art were all purchased to work with \u201dmy\u201d fireplace. It makes me happy. Photo of some original ancient petroglyphs:  And, some of mine:", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/7822542603be04f8_7501-w500-h700-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/f8826fd903be04fb_7499-w500-h326-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/5f6248b903be04fe_7509-w500-h148-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/b412741c03be0501_7521-w500-h145-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

It's an easy drive from Las Cruces as well.  Operated by the Bureau of Land Management, it's an absolutely magical look into the past and is home to approximately 21,000 (yes - twenty-one thousand!) petroglyphs in an area encompassing about two miles - literally everywhere you look, you'll spy rock art. title: Rootstock suckers on Meyer lemon tree? Where is the main trunk? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-66856988", "author_name": "Sarah S", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-66856988", "date": "2023-01-11", "text": "I'm attempting to revive this Meyer lemon tree I was recently given (you'll see previous pruning attempts in pictures below) and don't know where to start. I was told it was a tree, however the root system looks like there are three separate sections - what should I do? It's unclear which is the primary trunk of the tree, which aspects are rootstock suckers, and where to prune. Please help!", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/a1e2135c03bee04b_3761-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/7ba20a7403bee04d_3762-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2023-01-14", "text": "It's unclear whether the planting consists of several individual propagules, or the multiple trunks are all branches that connect to a lower order branch beneath the soil line. It could be either. If they are individual propagules, you can separate them when you next repot (spring), select one of the propagules, then remove any branches competing for position as the main leader so there is only 1 conspicuous trunk. If the lower branches were removed from this propagule such that all that remained is the cluster of branches at the top of the cutting, you could potentially end up with more than 8 trunks.  If you pruned off all branches except for 1 with the growing tip of the branch still attached, you would end up with a single-trunked specimen, and it wouldn't matter if the pruning was done before the propagule was stuck (in the grow medium) or at some later date.  If you live in the Northern Hemisphere and when you pruned, a large number of leaves were lost due to the pruning, it could be considered an error (from the plant's perspective). Leaves are each a food factory, working to produce the plant's true food (sugars/ starch). When the plant is pruned so leaves are lost, it increases the potential for the tree to be in a place where it is using more energy than it is creating (through photosynthesis). This is a dangerous position for a plant to be in as it is unsustainable; and, it puts the tree in a position where it must have enough stored energy reserves to push at least some new foliage to a point where it at least 75% mature, the break-even point where leaves change from being net users of energy to net producers. If you simply cut the 'extra' trunks off at the soil line, they will each back-bud from currently suppressed buds at or immediately below the soil line, which would add to the number of trunks/ stems on the plant. Al", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/0eb25bd503c2f48e_0978-w240-h180-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

title: The downside to extended large families | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "wittynicknamehere", "author_name": "WittyNickNameHere ;)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/wittynicknamehere", "date": "2023-01-11", "text": "I am a first generation Canadian.  While I was \"made in The Netherlands\", my parents immigrated to Canada with 2 daughters in tow, and were expecting me in a few short months (none of my relatives knew my mother was going on 4 months pregnant!). All in all, I had 3 aunts and uncles on moms side, and two of each on my dads side.  As for cousins, there were five on moms side, and 3 on dads.  One of the 3 on my fathers side took his own life in the early 80's, and his sister died about 8 years ago of a mysterious illness. I married a man with a huge extended family.  When I say huge, I mean HUGE!  His family has a lot of documented family history in this city as they are from the Tsuut'ina Nation which borders the city. With large extended family, comes a lot of fun family reunions.  My mother in law was big into taking pictures and I would sit for hours looking through all her photo albums learning about their family.  Who is related to who and how?  My mother in law and one of her sisters married brothers.  Two of their other sisters married brothers from another family.  When you live in a small small town, there's not a lot of people to choose from, you end up in the same family as your siblings.  LOL But with large extended family also comes a lot of sadness and grief.  Just in the last 18 months, my husbands first cousin lost her husband to suicide.  I knew him since I was 5.  Then a few months later, his mothers sister in law passed away.  This his mothers other sister in law passed away and a few days later, his mothers sister died.  His fathers sister died a couple months ago.  And today, I opened Facebook to see his cousins son died on the weekend. His death has hit me the hardest.  His mother and I were best friends for several years.  We drifted into different lives but still kept in touch through messenger and family reunions and funerals.  OMG, the last funeral we went to was for her cousin and it was like an episode from the Mary Tyler Moore show.  I couldn't stop laughing and literally had my face in my lap to keep from laughing out loud because of her.  It didn't help that her mother fell asleep in the middle of it all.  His mother died March 8 of 2014.  Her heart stopped while she was sleeping.  Her daughter found her.  I just got off the phone (I had to stop typing this because of the phone call) and her son called me to say he found his brother dead on the couch.  He died the same way his mother did.  Their hearts just stopped beating. I changed his diapers.  I babysat him while his mother went out to bingo.  I watched him turn into a terrific father who adored his son, and whose son idolized him. I love being part of a huge family.  But at the same time, I hate it.", "images": []}

title: Supprimer une cloison pour créer un espace : Bonne ou mauvaise idée ? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "influences-by-c-coataner-pfvwfr-pf~93318345", "author_name": "Influences by C. Coataner", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/interior-architects/influences-by-c-coataner-pfvwfr-pf~93318345", "date": "2023-01-13", "text": "Si la plupart des constructions neuves proposent aujourd\u2019hui un grand espace \u00e0 vivre avec une cuisine ouverte sur le salon et la salle \u00e0 manger, cette tendance n\u2019est plus r\u00e9serv\u00e9e uniquement \u00e0 la pi\u00e8ce principale. Alors que le dressing ose se montrer dans la chambre, la baignoire de la salle de bain s\u2019immisce dans l\u2019espace nuit comme pour mieux tirer ses habitants des bras de Morph\u00e9e. \u00c0 l\u2019heure de r\u00e9nover votre logement, vous h\u00e9sitez peut-\u00eatre \u00e0 tout casser. Quels sont les avantages \u00e0 faire tomber les cloisons ? Existent-ils des limites ? Et si d\u2019autres solutions existaient ? D\u00e9cryptage d\u2019un r\u00e9am\u00e9nagement \u00e0 faire tomber les murs !   Les avantages \u00e0 abattre une cloison : Moins de murs pour plus de lumi\u00e8re et d\u2019espace. Sous certaines conditions pour les murs porteurs d\u2019un logement, toutes les s\u00e9parations entre deux pi\u00e8ces peuvent en th\u00e9orie \u00eatre supprim\u00e9es. Cette redistribution de l\u2019espace r\u00e9pond \u00e0 deux objectifs principaux :1/ Agrandir la pi\u00e8ce principale2/ Faire entrer plus de lumi\u00e8re tout au long de la journ\u00e9e. \u21d2 Faire tomber un mur entre la cuisine et le salon permet de b\u00e9n\u00e9ficier de la lumi\u00e8re qui p\u00e9n\u00e8tre, par exemple, tant\u00f4t par la baie vitr\u00e9e, tant\u00f4t par la fen\u00eatre \u00e0 l\u2019oppos\u00e9. Moins de cloisonnement entre les pi\u00e8ces facilite \u00e9galement la circulation dans le logement. Plus besoin d\u2019ouvrir une porte ni de contourner la table de la cuisine. D\u00e9sormais, il suffit de passer d\u2019un c\u00f4t\u00e9 ou de l\u2019autre de l\u2019\u00eelot central pour se retrouver dans le salon ! main_question: {"author_id": "letstrydiy", "author_name": "letstrydiy", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/letstrydiy", "date": "2023-01-13", "text": "Good morning. We recently bought a home and discovered the retaining walls currently installed have no drainage behind them -- just dirt. Moreover, the grading behind the walls is pretty aggressive. We had some mudslides behind our home during these big California storms and are looking to improve the longevity of the walls without having to completely replace them, if possible. We are looking for some guidance. We've had some contractors come out and it's hard to tell if they're offering the best advice or just trying to create work -- I find them contradicting each other and proposing very different solutions. Our questions: Would appreciate any thoughts/guidance on the above.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/5642790c03c1423f_9793-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~1828811085", "author_name": "Verdance Landscape Architecture", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~1828811085", "date": "2023-01-17", "text": "Grading and retaining walls are complicated topics, so please forgive my essay here. (TL;DR: you're probably fine, but don't take my word for it.) Without seeing the walls and the slopes first-hand, it's very difficult to tell what the existing situation is and what, if anything, should be done. Take any advice you get here\u2014including mine\u2014with a large helping of salt; and always verify it with a licensed professional (landscape contractor, general contractor, engineer, landscape architect) on-site. To my eye, there's probably not much risk of a significant landslide around the walls in your photo. There just isn't a lot of mass behind them; I would be more concerned about the hillside between the hedge at the top and the fence at the bottom. The slope of the upper terrace (behind the top wall) looks fairly gentle, and the distance between the top and bottom walls looks relatively short although the slope is steeper. The walls appear to be constructed of interlocking concrete blocks, which are designed to lean back into the hillside for structural stability when stacked into courses like this. Yes, the walls should have been backfilled with crushed aggregate (\"drain rock\") wrapped in filter fabric; if you are sure this wasn't done, you could excavate horizontally a foot or so back from the wall, and vertically down to the footing. Installation methods vary but generally you'll want 6-12\" of topsoil and mulch at the top of the wall, then aggregate down to the level of the ground at the foot of the wall. A drain pipe at the lowest point won't hurt, assuming you have someplace even lower for it to drain away to (where the outfall won't cause erosion, which would destablize the slope); but some manufacturers say this is optional for walls less than 4' tall. A soils engineer could give you insights into how to handle the drainage given the characteristics of your particular soil. If you were going to add drainage to only one wall, I would suggest the lower wall, because I agree the grading between the top and bottom walls looks a bit aggressive. That slope appears to be around 1:1 (one foot of horizontal for every foot of vertical, or a 45\u00b0 angle); generally steeper than 2:1 (two horizontal for every one vertical, or a 27\u00b0 angle) is discouraged. That said, although the plantings look fairly new, I'm guessing the walls have been there for many years, and if the fill between them hasn't moved yet, it may be stable enough that no intervention is needed. Your hillside will always start at point A and end at point B, no matter how you regrade it. If you remove the top wall, the bottom wall would probably need to become taller, for which your town might require engineering plans and a construction permit. Removing soil between the top and bottom of the hillside is much more complicated than it sounds, because at some point your resculpted hill would have to connect back to the land around it, so then you might need retaining walls on the sides and/or the top. This is expensive, complicated, expensive, unattractive, and also costs a lot of money, so I wouldn't recommend it. Assuming the walls were properly constructed and the backfill is stable, the best thing you can do is maximize the plantings behind the walls and minimize the amount of water you apply. I don't know where in California you live, or what your sun exposure there is, but you could ask a local nursery to recommend noninvasive groundcovers (no Japanese honeysuckle, please!) that will not only shield the soil but also root as it spreads to prevent erosion. The creeping rosemary that's planted there now won't do this. Consider Salvia leucophylla, Mahonia repens, Symphoricarpos albus, Arctostaphylos uva-ursi, and other California native plants that put down deep roots. A web search for \"California native groundcover for erosion control\" will generate more ideas, like this page from the Theodore Payne Foundation. Nothing here should be taken as advice, only information. Recognize that sometimes the fastest way to destablize a slope is to start trying to stabilize it. Please proceed with all due caution. Good luck!", "images": []}}

title: Insurance pays for old roof to be replaced? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jehanne-hansen", "author_name": "claudia valentine", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jehanne-hansen", "date": "2023-01-13", "text": "So this guy comes knocking on my door offering to inspect my roof and , of course, to sell me a new one. There is no doubt that our roof is in need of replacing.  It has been there 23 years.  No leaks, but it is obvious that it needs attention, Hubs lets him up on the roof and, of course, he comes back down with the verdict that it needs replacing.  We knew that. But, here is the rub.  He tells us that he can get our insurance company to completely pay for replacing our roof, even if it is over 20 years old. He talks hubs into making a date to come back and take photos and detail what he says is wind damage.  Against my better judgment, Hubs, lets him. He comes back down with a series of photos of things all marked with chalk where there is \"damage\".   No doubt that there is.  It is old. Hubs invited him back to discuss doing this, and he came by yesterday and we sat down to talk. I looked up the roofing company  and I can find mostly all positive reviews.  I checked with the BBB and googled them.  Aside from the normal few folks who you would expect to have some complaints, of course, there were a few.  But, mostly glowing reviews online. So, I checked out where the company is based, who owns it, and checked the state licensing, and it all gives no red flags, at all. If not for the fact that this man is telling us that we can get our insurance company to completely cover the cost of replacement of our 20 year roof , I would find no obvious reason to not hire them. And, I do know for a fact that this company did the reroof for a neighbor, who also had a good recommendation.  I saw the company doing the work when they did it a short while ago because it is right outside of my kitchen window. So, I asked him why did he knock on our door. What he told me is that they have an employee who will research the area after a high wind event and target neighborhoods for age of the construction and then, I am guessing, that they send people out to actually take a visual assessment before they send someone like him to actually knock on the door. We did have a high wind event a couple of days before christmas. He says that there are a few insurance companies that will do this and Travelers is one that they work with a lot.  Allstate was one that does not do this, he said. He says that I file a claim and the insurance company will send out an adjuster.   He will meet the adjuster when the person comes to do the inspection. The only caveat is that we sign an agreement to actuallly hire them to do the work after the adjuster has approved it.  That makes me uncomfortable. So, is this guy for real?  I am skeptical.  He talks a good talk, but I dont want to be taken and I dont want to commit fraud. Everything that I read on the internet does say that an insurance company is not going to pay replacement for an old roof.  And, that would be my assumption, too.  Our insurance policy is one that does pay replacement cost, if needed due to damage by a \"peril\". He told me to file a claim and where it asks for the date of the damage to give the date of that high wind event that we had.   Now I suspect that this company pays attention to high wind events in order to market this, whether it is real or not. So, tell me, dear Houzz friends, does this sound right? I just see too many red flags no matter how nice of a guy he seems. He just promises too much. Has anyone actually had an insurance company replace an old roof with damage that happended over time? Somebody here must know something about this kind of thing. I am skeptical, but there is actually no real obligation on the part of either us or them until money has been exchanged. so I understand. I think that he promises too much for nothing. What do you think?  I am not comfortable with it, but, what if he is right?  You think, maybe? Hubs says that we have nothing to lose by trying, but I think that there is a something wrong somewhere.", "images": []}

The compressor is on or off.  As the laundry gets dryer there is less moisture to absorb the heat from the refrigeration cycle.  To keep the main re-heat coil at the proper temperature some of the refrigerant is diverted to the small radiator on the right side of the dryer. As stated above there is a variable speed van that blows over this radiator to remove the excess heat from the refrigerant.  This excess heat makes its way out of the dryer and into the room.  It is a small amount of heat.  Less than a freezer or refrigerator which moves all of the heat from the inside to the room. This is actually a very good thing as it keeps the air temperature inside the dryer consistent as the laundery approaches dry.  If the dryer did not have this then the laundry would get hotter as it gets dry.  Which is exactly what happens in a normal vented and most condenser dryers. The other option would be to use a variable speed scroll compressor.  These are significantly more expensive. title: Is Stock Overhyped? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "carolb-w_fl_coastal_9b", "author_name": "carolb_w_fl_coastal_9/10", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/carolb-w_fl_coastal_9b", "date": "2023-01-14", "text": "This article reflects my attitude toward making and using stocks. I often prefer water because I feel stock adds the wrong flavor. https://tastecooking.com/is-stock-overhyped/ The perfect base for your soup is flowing through your faucet. \"In the past, not having broth in my kitchen has been enough to stop  me from making soup. I believed stock was essential for making anything  that could be eaten with a spoon or sopped up with bread\u2014blame the  hundreds of offhand comments and cooking tips encouraging me to make my  own broth from whole chickens or frozen scraps like onion skins and  leftover bones. It\u2019s widely regarded by chefs and home cooks that  homemade stock outshines what\u2019s often sold in cartons and bouillon  cubes, but how many of us have the foresight to make stock in advance of  a soup craving? \u201cStock\u201d and \u201cbroth\u201d are terms that are often used interchangeably,  but they have slightly different meanings. Stock derives its flavor from  bones, while broth is made from simmering meat and vegetables in water.  Regardless, they both serve the same purpose: to act as the backbone of  flavor for all things stewed, saucy, and soupy. Until recently, I  wouldn\u2019t have dared to make my favorite tomato soup or risotto without  one of them on hand. Then I listened to an episode of the TASTE podcast with cookbook author Andy Baraghani,  who dismissed the notion that stock was necessary. In fact, he argued  that it could actually get in the way of a saucy dish\u2019s flavor, and he  advocated for using water instead. \u201cI have to say I use water [a] majority of the time over stock, and  it\u2019s really to allow the ingredients to shine,\u201d he says on the show.  \u201cWhether it\u2019s a nuoc cham or a braise, adding stock adds  weight\u2014unnecessary weight\u2014and I kind of want the freshness and that  clean water to allow the other ingredients to come through and breathe.\u201d... ...Baraghani acknowledges that stock has a place in many recipes, but he  says the idea that more ingredients equals more flavor can cloud whether  a recipe benefits from adding that flavorful base. \u201cStock can add that  extra layer: an extra layer of fat, an extra layer of umami, depth to a  braise, a dish, a soup that is sometimes needed,\u201d he says. \u201cBut on the  other side, it can also add an unnecessary layer when you want just a  few ingredients to shine.\u201d...\"", "images": []}

title: Currently contemplating build or buy existing. | Houzz Forum

We have about 70K saved to make this happen. We live in South Carolina and property/land sale prices are still high . We dont NEED alot of land, but probably at least an acre . Has anyone been our position recently and give some good learned advice? We have an income of of about 210K per year combined . My reasoning for buying land and building is, if youre going to pay a premium, pay it on what you want and something thats never been lived in. Is this faulty logic in 2023? Edit: I also wanted to mention both kids are out of the house as of June this year. One is already in college in Florida and the other ships out to Navy in June. main_question: {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2023-01-15", "text": "The roses aren't looking good.  I've been blaming myself for this, neglect, etc, but have recently been reconsidering.  I read a report on the weather yesterday in Repubblica which said that, of the five driest years since 1961, two were 2021 and 2022.  And it's been historically warm.  So far, this year isn't looking like it's going to be wetter, though of course it's early.  The reservoirs are low, water tables are low, there's no snowpack on the Apennines.  Normally, if one can still use that word, by this time of the year the world is drenched, sodden, dripping.  No more.  It's damp, but it's not wet. We had an awful drought in 2016-2017, too, lasting a year, and the roses came through that without difficulty.  I suspect, though, that this time we've hit the limit of what roses can take and still thrive.  I'm hardly looking at them, by the way, this fall, a combination of how depressing they are and having other projects on my mind, mainly the terracing of paths and general cleanup; plus, I've been sick since the start of the year and have little energy (trip to see the doctor tomorrow, to see what the illness is; it's not Covid).  The roses are hanging on, let me say, and some look fine, but this is definitely not their finest hour. Some plants are happy.  To restate our conditions:  Zone 8, chilly mild winters and hot summers, which used to be drier but we seem to be experiencing higher summer humidity than we used to.  Heavy gray clay soil on a southwest-facing steep slope, some areas of sedimentary rock close to the surface, neutral to alkaline Ph.  What's growing well.  Trees:  Italian cypresses; native downy oaks (deciduous) are seeding freely where shrubs have been in place for a while, while holm oaks, evergreen oaks native to further south in Italy, are good; flowering ash is a champion; laburnums are very tough: I have to see whether the slightly rooted suckers we planted will take; hazelnuts grow well if they have clay and are near water, i.e. a drainage ditch or in a low spot.  I have hopes for some young checker trees (Sorbus torminalis), suckers of which we dug up in the woods, and Chinese fan palms, seedlings from our trees at the house.  I'd love to plant the Mediterranean palm, Chaemerops humilis, but it's not so easy to find.  We have a flourishing wicked (it's a spiny beast) plant of it at the house.  Figs. I've been concentrating this winter on a part of the garden that we began in 2005, so eighteen years ago.  Plants have come and gone--roses in particular have gone--but what has lasted are mostly evergreen trees, shrubs, and subshrubs:  a Mediterranean look, an appearance more typical of central and southern Italy than of the north.  Well....I say that.  In fact, locally, olives, Italian cypresses, Italian pines, holm oaks, oleanders, bay laurel, are common, along with the deciduous wild flora and the temperate climate plants that are part of the garden repertoire around here.  Bay laurel is decidedly invasive. Ooof.  I've run out of steam.  And it's time to go out in the garden, cough and all.  To be continued later.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2023-01-20", "text": "Ingrid, what I'm thinking is that in the future we're all going to have less wiggle room to try plants that are marginal for our conditions.  I certainly understand your desire to have an oasis of flowering beauty and freshness, and hope that you may be able to create it, though it will be a struggle.  As climate change accelerates, swings from the average will become greater:  more rain when it rains, longer droughts when it's dry; lower lows, higher highs.  All this will increase risks to plants that are less well-adapted to the conditions they're growing in.  As I said, I'm currently wondering whether the less than thriving condition of a good many of my roses isn't due to our ongoing drought, unprecedented in my two decades' experience gardening here.  And yet quite a few plants are thriving.  I haven't given up on roses, heavens no, but I certainly am trying to mitigate the negatives of my conditions, amending the soil with organic matter and sand, planting, for shade, and for the other good things that come from plants.  In this way I can hope to grow my roses and many other loved plants better.  And at the same time, I'm observing which plants are rock solid under current conditions, and will be likely better to resist hard times when they arrive. main_question: {"author_id": "dimitrig-gw", "author_name": "dimitrig", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dimitrig-gw", "date": "2023-01-15", "text": "Hi, I have been raising 3 African violets I rescued from the garbage heap at Lowe\u2019s 3 years ago. They cost me $1 for the lot of them. I didn\u2019t even want them as they looked so bad, but my girlfriend convinced me to give them a chance.  I was skeptical that they would survive, but I managed to nurse them back to health and they have been thriving. The largest one is now 15 inches across and the next largest is 10 inches across. The smallest has lagged and is only about 6 inches across but it is the one that blooms the most. I bought them about 2 inches across in a thimble of a pot and about 1.5 years ago transplanted them to larger 4-inch pots. I water about once per week, sometimes less if the soil isn\u2019t super dry yet. I add a weak liquid violet fertilizer about every 3rd time. Two weeks ago I was surprised to see the smallest violet had droopy leaves that were brown at the edges. These were the oldest, biggest leaves on the plant. I sometimes remove old leaves as they age out so I removed a couple and checked back. A few days later they had gotten more brown and rotten looking and the green stems had started to turn to jelly. Fearing disease I cut off any leaves that looked even partially brown and stopped watering. Tonight I checked and even more leaves were falling victim and more stems were rotted. The stems remained green but were like jelly. I pulled the plant out of the pot and it hardly has any roots. I was expecting/fearing black rotted roots but was surprised to find almost none. There was just the taproot which still looked healthy enough and there are still a handful of healthy looking leaves. I cut away anything remotely gelatinous, dumped the soil, and repotted with the crown just touching the surface. Was that the right thing to do? Should I use some sort of anti-fungal or antibacterial? I am at a loss for why this one plant is afflicted. The others receive the same care and look fine - at least for now - although obviously their growth rates have differed so maybe this one has always been weaker. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-918119203", "author_name": "HU-918119203", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-918119203", "date": "2023-01-15", "text": "I asked a similar question recently and have since done more research, so this is my view. In my experience, mid-grade semi-custom cabinets, uninstalled, cost a lot more than true custom made-from-scratch cabinets from established, larger shops -- installed.  So for my kitchen, semi-custom cabinetry from Candlelight or TeddWood would be about $48k without installation.  Those are midrange lines.  While both have plenty of options, there's an upcharge for custom colors and I'd have to have many of the details (like brackets, open shelving, etc.) done separately, so add another $5-10k.  And then what - $5-10k for install?  So it's really $60-70k? My initial bid for all custom for the same kitchen was $30k, but that bid fell through.  New bids from very well-known, high-end makers in my high-end (Fairfield County, CT) area were all about $50k, installed.  And that was everything from soup to nuts, including any color I want and all the details my architect designed.  To me it's a no-brainer. People here will correctly tell you that you need to do research on the cabinetmaker and ask a lot of questions about what \"custom\" means to them, how cabinets are finished, etc. to determine the quality.  I'd argue you should ask most of the same questions when ordering semi-custom too.  The only other explanation I've heard for paying more for semi-custom is that these are established companies that will honor warranties if something goes wrong.  While that is a difference from a guy in a garage, a real established cabinetmaker will do the same, except you're dealing with someone down the street instead of in Pennsylvania or whatever. I sense on Houzz a skepticism of local cabinetmakers by (1) kitchen designers/store owners, who generally sell stock and semi-custom cabinetry for a living so have a vested interest and (2) homeowners who got burned looking for a super low price without doing their due diligence and then were shocked, shocked! when the quality wasn't great.", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "mr-bill_m", "author_name": "Bill M.", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mr-bill_m", "date": "2023-01-15", "text": "About two weeks ago I wandered into my local over priced nursery just to see what they had. I was amazed at the huge selection and variety of orchids. From oncidiums, to brassia to odonto to zygo, to paphs to phals to .... I had never seen them carry orchids like this before, just the common phals. Unfortunately they were priced from $40 on up, so I decided to pass, although  the Zygos did tempt me. Two days ago I went back again just to view them because it looked like an orchid show initially. To my surprise, over 80% of them had tags on them saying 50% off! I walked out with five different ones, but sadly, no zygos. Today I decided to repot all of them because they were in 4\" nursery pots. What a chore! They were grown in pure sphagnum moss, which was soaking wet. A lot of the roots on some were dead, whereas on others they were a combination of living and dead. It took forever to remove as much sphagnum as I could but it was a pure nighmare. I guess it's cheaper and easier to pot and grow in pure sphagnum for a bulk nursery, but I have to think that in the long run it doesn't do the plant any favors. What are your thoughts on this?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mr-bill_m", "author_name": "Bill M.", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mr-bill_m", "date": "2023-05-24", "text": "Just a quick update - Every orchid I purchased at 50% off is doing incredible!
