I can't do anything about the high daytime temps (there's shading on the polycarbonate, and a 50% shade cloth over the GH as well). The misting help somewhat, but not a lot. Since the roof is already lined with impervious sarking it is not clear to me if we can maintain breathability and therefore if it is worth using permeable insulation, cork boarding and lime plaster. To maintain ventilation is a 50mm gap enough or do we also need some vent rafters? From my research, it seems the best solution may be to use a multi foil insulation which is thinner and can be either breathable or non breathable. It's especially present when the boards are flat cut. When you stain the wood to get a medium color like your door, the grain turn black from the stain. Then we moved into the hallway and he asked me if I knew what colour it was. It was the same colour. title: Taking wood floor dark to light - dark stain remains in grain/joints? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "mqsterl", "author_name": "mqsterl", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mqsterl", "date": "2023-01-17", "text": "Calling all flooring experts!  We are taking our floors from a very dark color to a lighter, more natural finish - likely Bona Natural Seal or perhaps Duraseal Weathered oak.  When we booked the job, the flooring contractor did not mention any concerns about going from dark to light.  Today, he sent his guys over to put down samples, and one of them warned me that the very dark stain might not come out of the grain and that the joints between planks would remain darker.  The stain actually did come out of the grain pretty nicely, but the joints are indeed darker and more noticeble. Two questions: 1. Is this a well known, common issue when refinishing dark to light and just something I need to live with, or is this a skill/technique issue? 2. What if anything can be done to maximize how much the dark stain comes up/out of the wood and/or how much we can camuflage the darker joints so they are not as noticeable?  The flooring guy said that obviously going with a darker color, the darker joints will be less noticeable and I am therefore considering going with weathered oak or similar over natural seal for that reason.  However, if we didn't have this issue, I'd probably go with Natural Seal. Thoughts?? Thanks in advance!", "images": []}

title: Soil quality (under the parking lot) | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "tristansgarden", "author_name": "Tristan", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/tristansgarden", "date": "2023-01-17", "text": "Hi all, I posted a few weeks ago about converting a bus parking lot into an orchard.We got a few quotes to scrape off the top layer of soil. They came back high! That, plus the cost of new soil, is completely out of budget for us. We have to pick one or the other.Meanwhile we dug a hole in the gravel to see what we are working with. I have attached photos. It's not as bad as I thought it would be! Frankly it's no different from the quality of soil in the rest of the yard where there is lawn planted (the entire area is just fill dirt mixed with gravel) there are three mango trees and a coconut tree growing happily in this soil so I'm assuming it's not the end of the world if we don't remove it...? My only concern is going to all this expense and effort and then watching the trees fail to thrive.We talked to our neighbor who has an orchard himself, and he instructed us to not remove any soil but instead to bring in topsoil. He recommends at least two feet. This is due to the quality of the existing soil but also due to how marshy and wet the ground gets after a rain.Next we will do a soil test to learn if the soil is contaminated. \ud83e\udd1e", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/e961d70d03c71740_2007-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/85c1a05a03c71742_2008-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2023-01-18", "text": "And for a differing opinion......\ud83d\ude09 I would neither remove any soil nor would I import any topsoil.   What I see in the photos is soil that is devoid of much - if any - organic matter. And OM is critical in developing an active soil biology as well as providing the full range of nutrients plants need to thrive and be productive. And it will eventually improve soil structure and help with poor drainage. Instead, I would get my hands on as much compost or composted manures or any other OM as possible and topdress/mulch the planting area deeply. And I would do this at least one full growing season ahead of any planting to allow sufficient time for the OM to do its work. It could well be that the marshy or wet conditions after a good rain is due to heavy compaction - since it was a parking lot - so loosening the soil or aerating/reducing compaction would also be a priority, Contrary to poplar belief, asphalt is not a hindrance to successful plant growing, even with edibles. It occurs naturally (research bitumen), is heavily recycled and since petroleum based, is not take up by the plants. It generally has no adverse effect on plant growth (unless it's smothering them :-)) But like the previous comment, I see no obvious signs of asphalt present.", "images": []}}

title: Why does the sink need to be close to the fridge? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "cevamal", "author_name": "cevamal", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/cevamal", "date": "2023-01-18", "text": "I was reading another post where it was mentioned and it got me wondering. I'm not saying put it in another room, but in my regular workflow having the sink and fridge close doesn't seem to matter. What's important to me is having the sink close to the prep sink. I take things out of the fridge and yes, I may need to wash them, but I usually need to open a package or bag or something first. Plus it's been in the fridge so it's not dripping anywhere so saving a few steps doesn't matter. Eventually I get the produce to the sink and wash it, but then I have dripping produce I need to get to my prep area. This is what makes me crazy and why I am so excited to have a prep sink in my next kitchen. (Currently my single sink is on the perimeter and my main work area is an island.) What am I missing? Why is this generally considered a priority?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "stm25rs", "author_name": "stm25rs", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/stm25rs", "date": "2023-01-18", "text": "I personally think some of the \"work triangle\" thinking (which is probably the origin of whatever post you're referencing) is a bit outdated, especially with larger, more open kitchens, and kitchen islands that are often hubs for more than just cooking. Googling \"kitchen work triangle outdated\" returns a bunch of blog posts that match my thinking, so apparently I'm not the only one. I spend the vast majority of my kitchen time prepping, and at my range. I'm not making frequent trips to the refrigerator since I get out any fridge ingredients all at once. I wash/dry my produce when I bring it home from the store, before putting it in the fridge, so I'm not bouncing back and forth between my fridge or prep space or sink. My cooking prep is chopping and measuring ingredients, and rarely involves the sink. You know your cooking workflow, just keep that in mind while thinking about your layout. Since you'll have a prep sink, that gives you even more flexibility.", "images": []}}

title: Living next to a small private school temple combination, 4 churches? | Houzz Forum

I wrote 'next to' instead of near because some of the lots are across the street or adjacent to these places, but not all of them are. I do plan to spend some time walking around the neighborhood when they have events, but wanted to get some perspective here as well. We are interested in the houses on this block because they are 2-3x the typical lot size for an urban area. Some of the lots are across the street from the temple/school, and others are adjacent or back up to the churches. Two lots are across the street from one church. Access to the temple/school is on the same road as two of the churches, then another church is around the corner. We aren't religious so would not be attending services, but we do have a family member with developmental disabilities who currently works at a similar school in a different location, so if he could find a job there, it would be beneficial. Resale is some concern but ideally we would live here for the rest of that family member's life at least. The private school + temple has about 120 parking spaces and an enrollment of about 80-125 kids. It's been around for a very long time and I don't see it going anywhere due to a fairly strong temple community. They have one long bus and three shorter buses which are not typically parked in the parking lot closest to the houses we're looking at (parking for the buses is at the back of the school). Looking at their calendar they seem to have quite a bit of programming, with smaller groups meeting Tues-Thu in the late afternoon/evenings, and larger groups meeting Friday nights and Saturday mornings. Pics on social media show attendance at around 30-50 people for the Friday/Saturday groups. It's located at one end of the block, and then on the other end is two churches on adjacent corner lots, both with relatively small congregations. One church has about 100 parking spaces and the other it's hard to tell because the lot is gravel and mostly unmarked, but maybe 60-100 spaces. Online it looked like both churches had around 20-30 people in attendance for services. One seems to be kind of struggling for funding and the other has in recent years sold off some of its adjacent land to a couple that built a house on the lot. The third church is directly across from the temple/school with about 70 parking spaces, and there's no online presence so no info at this time. The fourth church isn't directly close to most of the lots of interest, but worth mentioning anyways because it has about 240 parking spaces. Online pictures show about 40 people in attendance at services. I've attached a crudely drawn map that hopefully clarifies things. It should be self explanatory but the little white rectangles are to show where the parking lot access is to the various facilities. Busses run down the black roads with the thickest being major arterials and the thinner black roads being minor arterials. Everything else is a narrower neighborhood road. Up is north. Any thoughts or experiences would be greatly appreciated, thank you!", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/2502b69803c8718b_0699-w500-h277-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

I'm working with a KD, and as we did the plans, she seemed to have in mind a particular cabinet line, a lower-priced one that she sells, which is fine because other cabs she sells go up to very pricey custom European brands. I was initially apprehensive about working with her because I didn't want to be stuck buying super-expensive cabinets. But my architect is used to working with her, and in our initial meeting I liked her approach, and the ballpark estimate she gave for cab cost seemed doable. However, my intuition may now be proving correct. This is for a new custom build, and I want the wood cab doors to have a natural finish and look that complements the floors (which will be a different stain but the same species). I'm finally at the point where it's time to look at door samples, and guess what, I didn't like any of them in the cab line the KD had in mind.  The wood looks and feels almost like laminate, with a very artificial-looking surface, and there is a very limited choice of stains, all of which add colors to the wood that make it look unnatural, white-ish or pink-ish. The \"best\" one is too orange. I didn't think finding a white oak door with a natural-looking stain would be a big ask. But apparently this particular cab line is more focused on their painted doors. They'll match any paint color, which is fine for the cabs I plan to paint (although frankly I don't love the very uniform paint finish vs one that shows brush strokes, I can live with it--it's more modern than my aesthetic, I think, even though the house is modern-ish). I did find a wood door I like very much, but guess what? It's in the next cab line up, which will probably be a lot more $$. (15-30% more.) I feel kind of bait-and-switched right now, even though I don't think this was an intentional thing on the KD's part. I'm advance freaking out about the cost. I  thought maybe I'll do all painted cabinets instead (not excited about that). Or maybe I could reduce the number of wood cabinets if I need to lower the cost. I asked if we could do a combo of two different manufacturers, one for paint and the other for wood, and the person I was working with wasn't sure. On the other hand, I can't help thinking that there are a gazillion cabinet companies, and I have to believe there is a mid-priced option for white oak slab doors that look natural, and if the price turns out to be unreasonable where I am, I could try to find another company. The other idea would be to see if the custom cabinet shop my builder works with could supply the wood cabinets. Either way, I'd have to do the kitchen design all over again, because I can't keep it, and I'd lose the retainer, but I think that would be fair given the work the KD did on the design, and it would still be a fraction of the difference in cabinet costs. But that seems like a \"nuclear\" option, and another solution would be better. Has anyone else had this problem? If so, what did you do? Suggestions?", "images": []}

If you are going to the added expense of applying a stone finish then don't shortchange yourself and regret not doing it properly every time you walk past it or are there enjoying your fireplace. A couple of rules to go by with stone. 1. If you are going to make a feature of something the clad the entire feature not half of it, otherwise it will look like you ran out of money - how embarrassing! 2. Always think in 3D. Natural stone is a 3D material and should be applied to all exposed surface not just one. I have seen columns clad only on the street face and it looks so cheap. Trust me - don't go there. DO NOT finish one face with a raw edge and start the next face - again it looks so fake. There are three basic ways that you can treat an external corner so it looks real. (i) Mitre the corners so with half or 1/3 rd 2/3rds tiles or stone. You the start the second face with the balance of the sheet that when mitred to the first sheet looks as one solid piece of stone. (ii) Finish the stone hard up against another element that will conceal the raw edge. (iii) Select a stone that comes with a specially cut corner tile. These are usually natural stone that have been had the back specially cut out to form an \"L\" for the corner. ECO OUTDOORS offer a selection of stone walling with the corner stone. title: Reducing heat above gas fireplace insert | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "austindlee", "author_name": "Austin Lee", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/austindlee", "date": "2023-01-19", "text": "Hi there- I'm looking to get some advice on how to reduce the heat on the surface directly above our new gas fire place insert.  We just finished the upgrade and really love the look and design (see photo), but the surface is so hot (250-270 F) that it's cracking the mud and plaster in more than one place (only one is on a seam)   Here are the details: The unit is a Valor G4 with no fan The surface of the fireplace was prepped with hardibacker, glued and screwed to the sub structure with a hot mud float to even out the surface. Venetian plaster applied to finish. Looking for suggestions/advice to make sure we're using the right materials to prep the surface before the plaster is applied and also to reduce the heat on the surface above the fireplace.  Obviously we can turn down the flame to lower the temp, but it would be great to have the option of using all the features of the gas insert and not have to limit its flexibility. Thanks in advance for the advice and suggestions.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/b422cbfe03c981ee_0384-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~2047579894", "author_name": "Hansen Wholesale", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~2047579894", "date": "2023-01-22", "text": "@Beth H. : One of the main questions that Austin Lee asked was: \"...how to reduce the heat on the surface directly above our new gas fire place insert \". Redoing the wall with metal studs, etc as Wacky Tacky has suggested would be the proper method for plastering the wall (and I agree). However,  it will not reduce the surface temperature of the wall, although the plaster will be less likely to crack. Adding a hood (also called heat deflector) can in fact reduce the heat on the plaster surface significantly, so I'm not sure why you are saying it will not. The hood will deflect the heat out towards the room instead of going directly straight up the wall, giving it a moment to mix with room air, which occurs quickly. I'm not sure why you are saying it won't help. Hoods have been used as heat deflectors for fireplaces for many years. In fact, most ventless gas fireplace manufacturers include them with their units and they cannot be installed without them if there is a combustible wall surface above the fireplace. Ventless gas fireplaces push 100% of the heat into the room, so they are even more problematic than a direct vent fireplace such as the Valor G4 insert. @Austin Lee I recommend you do a simple test by creating a mock hood (heat deflector) using a couple 2x4s with a piece of sheet metal screwed on top as illustrated below. I would test it with both 4\" and 6\" wide pieces to see if there is much difference between them. Get yourself an infrared thermometer to check the wall temperature at various heights above the fireplace with and without the mock hood. Here's how the mock device might look shown taped to the wall. You need to make sure the sheet metal is flush to the wall so no heat gets between it and the wall. Maybe tape it there as well.   I guarantee you will find a significant difference in the wall temperature during this test. I would not be surprised if it was as much as 50%. An actual hood will perform better due to the construction at an angle with a leading edge. And to your point Beth, yes, the hood will get very hot to the touch just as the other components of the fireplace as described in the owner's manual. With that said, it is also possible to fabricate a hood that is insulated to reduce the heat at the top surface, although I have yet to see an insulated hood offered on the market, I'd be happy to design one.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/d262b32503cdcdf2_1986-w240-h320-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

title: Homeowner insurance information | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "rachiele-custom-sinks-pfvwus-pf~562163075", "author_name": "Rachiele Custom Sinks", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/kitchen-and-bath-fixtures/rachiele-custom-sinks-pfvwus-pf~562163075", "date": "2023-01-19", "text": "We recently had a major flood due to a plumbing leak caused by a plumber recommended by our contractor during the remodeling of three bathrooms in our home. Much to my surprise, our homeowner insurance immediately denied the claim. Apparently, written into most policies, they will not cover poor workmanship. We had to go after the plumbers insurance policy. These are a few of the caveats you should be aware of. Third party insurance does not replace item for item. They depreciate everything. Secondly, if you decide to get an attorney involved, attorney fees are NOT recovered if you win. They are if you go after your homeowner policy! Most importantly, find a reputable public adjuster. Ours got us significantly more than we would have gotten on our own. Lastly, if you discover a leak, tend to it quickly. If you let it go a while, no insurance will likely cover it.", "images": []}

(Long story short, ship date will not be changed.) The reason Marble is not really suitable for Kitchen benchtops is that it is a soft stone that can scratch from the heard wear inflicted on a kitchen benchtop, plus it is porous so it will stain from many of the ingredients used in a kitchen and it will also mark from acidic foods and many household cleansers. It is for these reasons why alternative material which still look like Marble are generally used and recommended for Kitchen Benchtops. Quartzite for example is still a natural Stone, which in some forms like  Bianco Superiore Quartzite ,  Taj Mahal Quartzite ,  White Pearl Quartzite, Sky White Quartzite and Calacatta Mont Blanc Quartzite, all form with distinctive veining; much the same as Marbles have. Quartzite is better suited for Kitchen tops though because it is as hard wearing as Granite, is Acid Resistant, and is Stain Resistant. Alternatively, man made Reconstituted Stone products (also called Engineered stone or Quartz Tops) are made from a mix of quartz particles and resin which comes in a huge range of Look-Alike Marble Styles, where this product type is also more hard wearing and stain resistant than real Marble. Likewise Man Made Sintered Porcelain Slab Manufacturers also make a variety of Marble Look-Alike styles. All these products have a place in the market and each can fill specific design requirements that another material type may not be able to do, so it is well worth doing your homework on their individual characteristics & specifications so to better guide your material choice to best suit your specific application and needs. I bought a second one for downstairs WC. title: Sketchup Noob designs kitchen. What would it Cost? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "umpar-soze", "author_name": "Sarem mukhtar", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/umpar-soze", "date": "2023-01-21", "text": "Houzz pros! Need your help. Budget for the kitchen is between $50-75,000, not including appliances. This is not a DIY! Corner cabinet will have a lazy susan. Cabinet fillers or decorative legs bordering the side of the range and sink can be pulled out and will have storage functions for small items like spices, utensils, cutting boards and small cleaning accessories. 3x5 Island will have electrical outlets with usb ports, slide out garbage cabinet, cutlery drawer, vegetable cabinet, and a large cabinet below the cutlery drawer for storing things like plastic boxes or large dishware. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "buehl", "author_name": "Buehl", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/buehl", "date": "2023-01-21", "text": "Regarding \"cost\"...The rangehood alone will be quite expensive -- decorative ones like that are not cheap.  You've designed a high-end Kitchen, not a mid-range Kitchen.  Wood species & finish, fixtures, counter materials (butcher block? Other?), decorative elements, etc., will all affect the cost.  Without more info, even those living in Seattle may not be able to give you a ballpark/guess as to whether it's enough. Is anything else included?  Kitchen flooring?  Changing/adding/removing windows, walls, or doors/doorways in the Kitchen? Regarding spice storage below the counter -- we did that and ended up moving all the spices to an upper cabinet b/c they were too low to be easily accessed.  Some people put them in drawers (in the top position) as well.  We're a tall family, so the upper cabinet (a middle shelf) works for us. For the corner upper, get an easy-reach with a pie-cut shape rather than a diagonal cabinet.  Those diagonal cabinets reduce the \"face/head\" space in the corner, an issue because you have very little space b/w the rangetop and sink, which is prime real estate/counterspace for prepping (b/w your only water source and the rangetop).  In addition, storage is too deep to be useful in a diagonal cabinet and will be difficult to keep tidy looking (glass doors). Your prime prep space is too small -- you need at least 36\" of continuous counterspace b/w the sink and rangetop (either side of the corner).  Your ovens are taking up needed counterspace. Right now, most of your counterspace is in the island, which will not be particularly useful for prepping because of the lack of a water source in the island. If you put a sink in the island, then the lack of counterspace b/w the rangetop and sink will not be that big of an issue b/c that's not where you'll be prepping. Note that KEY components of a functional/successful Prep Zone are: Also important, but not as important as the above 3 items, is the trash pullout in the Prep Zone but easily accessible to the Cleanup Zone. For functionality...My recommendation is to either put a sink in your island or get a range instead of a rangetop + ovens and then move the range to the left to provide at least 36\" b/w the range and right corner. For cost...go with a simple stainless steel range hood instead of the decorative one and eliminate the pot filler (not very useful in the long run -- no drain to empty pots or to catch leaks/drips and you still have to carry pots of water from the range to the sink for dumping). main_question: {"author_id": "bonsai-citrus_and_indoor_gardening", "author_name": "bonsai_citrus_and_indoor_gardening", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bonsai-citrus_and_indoor_gardening", "date": "2023-01-22", "text": "I know that I can't be the only one who has struggled with this, so I thought I'd create a discussion topic for it. Some background for those who haven't seen any previous posts by me. I've been growing citrus for a number of years exclusively indoors. All of my trees grow well, are healthy, and fruit in their window. (I also grow a couple bonsai trees in other rooms). My question is a bit connected to a rangpur lime seedling I was given a few years back. Because this tree is one of only two trees that were grown from the seed of a special tree belonging to my grandmother, I can't give it away. I would like to eventually let this tree grow to the same size as my Nagami and Fukushu which are both about 4 ft tall and have large, spreading canopies. At the moment, however, I am very limited on space. My growing area is about 2 ft deep by 15 feet wide and is home to about 12 large air plants, three orchids, a fukushu, Nagami, and Nancy garrison passion vine (this one is huge and regularly tries to take over my window), a rangpur lime, a makrut lime, a fig tree, and seedlings of sour orange, tangelo, and indo mandarinquat. The rangpur lime was previously a very sick, very tiny seedling in a 2 inch pot which I was given in the hopes that i could save it from root rot and a number of deficiencies that were killing it. By last year it was about 8 inches tall, had three branches, and very green leaves. It smells amazing. But now, it has grown to about 13 inches tall and spreads about 2 feet in all directions. It has about 9 new branches sprouting, which are growing rapidly and it is quickly overtaking the small space I have for it to grow. In the next few weeks I'll be repotting a bunch of my trees (I finally found the full-size pot I plan to keep my fukuhsu in, so I'm going to play some musical pots. Fukushu into new pot and makrut lime into fukushu pot). My question is this: I want to eventually grow the rangpur to the size of the fukushu and Nagami, and I'd love to see it fruit sooner rather than later, but I can't until I move from my current home and have more space to grow plants. It is doing very well finally, so I don't want to mess with it too much, but it is also somewhat root bound in the tiny 8 inch pot it lives in right now. If I pot it into a bigger pot, I'll have to put it on the ground, where it will get less light than it gets currently so it might not do as well, but then again it might do just fine as there is quite a bit of light where I can place it. So here are my choices: 1. Repot the rangpur into the former makrut lime pot (12 inch), move it to the ground and let it grow. 2. root prune the rangpur, wire the branches to get them out of the way, prune it, and then return it to the 8 inch pot. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "remodeling1840", "author_name": "remodeling1840", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/remodeling1840", "date": "2023-01-23", "text": "One thing that helped me was visiting historic and accurately designed house the same era as mine.  Benjamin Moore has Historic Colors Williamsburg collections of appropriate colors ( yes, I know Colonial Williamsburg is a decade before the OP\u2019s house) but these colors are compatible with your house.   The magazine Early American Life is a good resource.  Years ago we had Colonial Homes and other magazines that seemed intent on maintaining historical context.  I am afraid white wouldn\u2019t be appropriate except for wall colors.  Your colors are spot on for the era\u2026.sorry!  Some of the places to visit would be Pleasant Hill, KY, a Shaker village ( the Shakers were quite active during your exact time period), Locust Grove, Louisville, KY, Colonial Williamsburg, VA, Winterthur, PA, Sturbridge Village, and Adena, Chillicothe, OH.  Call your local historical society if you are new to the area and find homes in your area that are restored.  Our house was built in 1803 and our goal is to honor the house and the man who built it.  Yes, we do have electricity, indoor plumbing, and cable tv, but my original plaster walls and woodwork are our pride and joy.  I cook in my six foot wide fireplace and on my six burner Thermador, but the six foot high doors in the library and dining room will not be raised in my lifetime.  People can duck.  We have decided that there is no rush on design decisions for our house-it\u2019s 220 years old and patient.  I will personally haunt any future owner who wants this house to be \u201copen concept\u201d!", "images": []}}

title: On becoming a better caretaker of our elders ... | Houzz Forum

My parents are in their 80s and while still sound mentally and active socially and otherwise (they do a bit of traveling here and there), they have dealt with some physical issues over the past couple of years that have taken a certain toll and required me to step in as the only adult child who lives near them and is thus able to offer immediate assistance.  I consider it a privilege to help care for these people whom I love dearly and who have bestowed so much care upon me throughout my life.  I also find the entire fact that this is even happening quite daunting, emotionally laden, and frightening at times. I am quite sure that these feelings are common. Due to health limitations and a desire to withdraw from certain social circles that no longer meet their needs, my parents' world is constricting - and they realize this.  They're going through emotions of their own dealing with inevitable decline, and I try to come alongside them to listen empathically.  It isn't always easy.  There are many times that I feel my own resistance to reality rising up, as though I can possibly stop the future from unfolding.  It's a childlike/childish longing for nothing to change, and for life to be strong and sweet -- as I remember from my childhood.  Of course nothing stays the same.  Time marches on.  It's happening ... and I want to get my head around it and prepare.  Maybe it's reality that nothing can really prepare you, but I also have to think that just having an awareness that there is further decline and loss and grief on the horizon has got to be a pragmatic help in some way.  We can't escape the inevitable. So ... have you experienced any of these feelings, or anything similar, and have you found anything that has been a help to you?  I've thought about having a few therapy sessions, perhaps.  I know too that there are groups that meet to discuss these things -- but I don't feel entirely comfortable going that route. title: Why is my relief valve leaking | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-810842943", "author_name": "Tim Atlas", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-810842943", "date": "2023-01-25", "text": "So i purchased a home which had not been in use for a couple years, and upon moving in i discovered the water heater relief valve leaking excessively. Its pretty new, house was built in 2018. I replaced the relief valve, as well as both elements and vaccumed out what calcium i could from the bottom with a tiny hose. It is still consistently leaking after all this. What else could be the problem?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "klem1", "author_name": "klem1", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/klem1", "date": "2023-01-26", "text": "Excessive pressure on water supply and/or improperly installed back-flow device.   Put a pressure gauge on a hot water outlet to see if pressure exceeds rated pressure of T&P valve.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "jakethewonderdog64", "author_name": "Jake The Wonderdog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jakethewonderdog64", "date": "2023-01-26", "text": "Klem is correct. A T&P valve opens because of temperature or pressure.  Almost always a leak or drip is excessive pressure unless there's crud under the seat of the valve. But if you've replaced it, you've ruled out crud on the seat. Excessive pressure typically happens for two reasons: 1. The incoming water pressure is too high. If that's the case, you need a pressure reducing valve. Excessive water pressure can damage pipes, valves, appliances and the water heater. 2. There is already a pressure reducing valve on the main line (and it's working properly) but there's no expansion tank on the water heater. A PRV works as a backflow valve also, so when your water heater heats the water, there's no place for it to expand to if there's no expansion tank or the tank isn't working. This results in temporary excessive pressure. Both situations are very hard on your plumbing. The T&P valve is a safety... don't ignore the underlying issue.", "images": []}}

title: Advice on kitchen undercabinet replacement lighting | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "partim", "author_name": "partim", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/partim", "date": "2023-01-25", "text": "We currently have fixtures with 4 fluorescent bulbs under our kitchen cabinet uppers, and want to switch to LED. There seem to be so many options - bulbs, strips etc. We'd appreciate any advice before we call an electrician. Also, we have no light above our stove,  just a fan. Can we add one?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/c6a2406f03d1b87f_8784-w500-h333-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/25126c8d03d1b87f_8784-w500-h418-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "3onthetree", "author_name": "3onthetree", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/3onthetree", "date": "2023-01-26", "text": "You could replace the fluorescent with LED 'bulbs' if you want. I suspect your UCLs are T5's @12\" or shorter. I am only familiar with 4' T8/T12 swaps, and I personally would only do direct wire (meaning you bypass the ballast) - because to me that is the achilles heel of fluorescents with frustration - the ballast (ballast going out usually forces people to convert to LED because ballast is so expensive!). But I don't know how expensive T5 direct wire are (or if you can even get them that small) - so evaluate whether swapping in a new LED fixture would be cheaper/easier. The hood, that's certainly an old fan unit. With all the exposed wood I don't think it would cause cleanliness problems putting a fixture under there. Maybe an 18\" or 24\" LED direct wire linear fixture, as slim as you can find (the really slim are only plug-in). Mount it inside of the front of the hood, with an MC cable from the fan j-box to the light, so it'll be switched along with the fan. **T5 fluorescent tube is 5/8\" dia, really skinny, UCL from 1990s+ usually have them at 9\" long or 12\" long.", "images": []}}

The reason for that is, organic media components require large populations of soil organisms to break down soil particles into a form plants can absorb, but container culture is generally not conducive to stable populations of soil biota. Also, high activity of soil life speeds breakdown of a medium's structure, which is a critical part of maintaining roots in good health. Regular applications of an appropriate fertilizer is an essential part of maximizing plant's opportunity to realize as much of their genetic potential as possible. Foliage-Pro 9-3-6 is an excellent choice as a 'go to' fertilizer for houseplants, and supplies a complete nutritional supplementation from a single container. title: Roses in South Florida Zone 10b Humid: Pot or Plant? Own Root/Graft? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-43509494", "author_name": "Kimberly Wendt (Florida Z. 10b)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-43509494", "date": "2023-01-27", "text": "Hi all, I'd like to get your opinions please! Questions listed at the end. First some background: I'm setting up a new tropical 'cottage' rose garden, here in south Florida, 10b humid. Front of a north/northeast facing house. Area roughly 50' x 50' overall, but only 25' x 50' is remotely suitable for roses. Rest is too shaded. Going with an informal, mixed color style (staying away from reds), organic, turning paths w/ curving or circular beds drifting between. I'll be able to get to all sides of each rose bush for pruning later. Sun/Soil/Structures: Been tracking the sun for weeks. Best area gets full to full/dappled 8am to 3pm. Soil is about 4\" deep then starts mixing in with sand. pH=6.4 prior to amending. Amending with my own compost, banana peels, coffee grinds, alfalfa pellets, black cow, mushroom compost and organic potting mix. Monterey's Nematode Control, followed by application of beneficial nematodes as a soil drench. No plants planted yet. Structures in the plan: 80 x 90 free standing trellis, standard arbor, three 8' tall metal obelisks and various little focal point do dads. I had tried establishing a formal rose garden in the back (southern exposure, full sun) about 5 years ago. Used mostly high teas on fortuniana, in ground. Black spot, not enough water even with every other day drip irrigation, too hot/scorched roses. Only thing that lived over a year was LD Braithwaite... and the root stock. Finally shoveled it and gave up. Since I've had to remove most of the landscaping and trees on the front of house... now seems like a good time to try again. Differently. Front yard tended toward growing ferns... a lot more moist, better soil, a lot of shade. Much of the shade is gone now, having removed 6 massive areca palms. This time, thinking to do own root, shrubs and hardy OGRs. Polyculture, mixed plants. Organic and provide some afternoon shade as well. See if these changes can make the difference. On Order: 11 own root/bare root David Austins: Generous Gardener,Claire Austin, James Galway, Lady of Shalott, Vanessa Bell, Qn of Sweden, Ancient Mariner, Windermere, Poet's Wife, Scepter'd Isle, and Olivia R Austin. All these were suggested/approved by DA themselves for 10b humid and shady, north facing situations (several conversations with DA US AND UK). Have 2 store bought Zepherine Drouhin for the large trellis as that's near the  walkway in the far corner, away from the other roses. I love her, but she's a black spot maven. The plan calls for generous spacing, more than mature widths - leaving room for more airflow, other plants, annuals to fill in while the roses grow larger, some perennials mixed in... mixed borders/beds 1/2 roses and 1/2 everything else. 1. Am I on the right track? Proponents say that going organic, letting the roses live in polyculture ecosystems, with beneficial insects, clean care, etc. makes for healthier plants. 2. Own root vs Fortuniana? There is so much talk about using Fortuniana root stock, but for me it creates shallow rooted roses, that drink a lot. Even staking they were easily blown over. Proponents of own root cite deeper roots, (longer establishment times). There is much buzz about root knot or gall nematodes in or soil, that fortuniana is the answer. Some say answer is own root. ???  Many people on this forum say that roses in 10b will grow like crazy big.... and I have a small yard. I don't need 35' towering house-eating roses.... I need smaller, healthier ones. I think? What do you all think? Recommend? 3. In Ground or in Pots? Since I'm getting own root.... in ground or in pots? Again, some rosarians warn against going in ground because of nematodes. They recommend huge pots, up off the ground on feet. Really HUGE pots! I could cut 55 gallon plastic drums in half making a pot that's 18\" deep by 23\" diameter. Even spray painted in nice pale colors, still not the most charming look.... lol. Can't really disguise them as urns or terracotta pots no matter how much paint I use... lol. I shudder to think of finding a pot for Generous Gardener... grin. Or, a few other rosarians say it's okay put them in the ground, so long as you do organic, own root  and the natural resistances of the rose will rise to the occasion. Some say don't put in the ground UNLESS they are on fortuniana roots. Sigh..... ? What do you think? 4. What other OGR/Shrubs should I consider? The plan has several 'holes' and even sections that are blank - to expand a bit later. I know Austins, but I don't know the millions of OGR and the like. What about miniature or small roses - like the Drift series? OGRs, repeat bloomers, fragrant, etc. What would your recommendations be for a shady, north facing, 10b humid garden? Phew! I need a coffee after all of that. If you've actually read through this tome and offer suggestions, ideas, advice or commiserations - I thank you and highly appreciate it! Regards, Kim", "images": []}

main_question: {"author_id": "3katz4me", "author_name": "3katz4me", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/3katz4me", "date": "2023-01-27", "text": "I know we've talked about guest rooms in the past but I just got back from staying with friends for four nights so I was thinking about this again - what makes a nice room for guests.  I suppose I'm into that since we have lots of guests at our lake cabin. Of course this is obviously a first world problem. We really prefer not to stay in someone's home but sometimes you just have to and it is much more convenient and fun to hang out with good friends and of course family.  We have a couple good friends we always stay with when we visit.  They have no one living with them - just the couple themselves. The thing that strikes me most about both of these places is how much stuff is on every surface in the guest room.  As a guest you come with all your stuff and there isn't a single surface where you can put it - including no bench or luggage rack for your luggage. I felt a bit weird this time when I removed all the stuff on the dresser and night tables and put it under the tables or under the bed.  The bed had all kinds of decorative pillows that of course had to be removed and really nowhere to put them but piled up on the floor. There was a large walk-in closet where you might have hung some clothes but it was being used for storage so we couldn't get to the hanging area.  This was a casual trip so we didn't really need to hang much as long as we could take stuff out of the suitcase and lay it in piles somewhere so we didn't need to keep taking things in and out of the suitcase on the floor.  I thought maybe I was expected to put it in the dresser drawers but they were full.  We had the luxury of an ensuite bathroom but it was tiny with no surface area for personal items so had to find a place to put that stuff too.  These people have a lot of overnight guests and I'm kind of surprised it isn't setup more with that in mind but I guess that's because that's the way I have our lake place.  Luggage racks in each room, nothing on the surfaces other than bedside lamps and a clock, closets accessible and equipped with hangers. There are some things you like just because of personal preference and some things that the host can't do anything about - the size of the bathroom for example.  I do think though that if you have guest rooms used exclusively for guests - no resident use - that the surfaces should be uncluttered with nik naks, artificial plants/flowers, etc. and if you have decorative pillows on the bed you either need a place where they can be stored when the bed is in use or they should be removed before guests arrive.  That's what I do with our guest room at home.  I take all the fru-fru stuff off the bed before the guests arrive.  We are fortunate to have large guest bathrooms with good vanity surface area but I still have nothing on there except a few disposable glasses, hand soap, lotion and I always have kleenex somewhere in the bathroom. Okay - off my soapbox now.", "images": []}

Only to find out I can't wear them most of my days, I have to crook my neck to be able to see the computer screen, can't sit like that 9-10 hours a day.  So something needs to be done about that situation; more on that below. I've been wearing the progressives on my non-work days and they're ok but not without problems.  My distance vision is crystal-clear, but I don't like that I seem to have lost some peripheral vision (it's kinda blurry), which concerns me because I drive a lot in the dark and have enough trouble seeing at night as it is, I'm afraid I'm going to take somebody out because my clear field of vision isn't as wide.  Most of my doings around the house are more of an intermediate distance (cooking, cleaning, gardening, etc).  Any reading I do without glasses -- I always have, ever since I was a kid I've found it far more comfortable to read with my glasses off and the reading material up close.  I wonder if a bifocal would be better because the peripheral vision would be clearer and I wouldn't have to keep moving my head around to focus clearly on something or maybe just a single vision for intermediate and another single vision for distance (for driving) because I usally read without glasses anyway. So I have to decide what to do because these are useless for my workdays.   My vision plan allows for a separate pair of computer glasses, so I figure these are my options: *  Keep these progressives and get a separate pair of progressive computer glasses (made specifically for computer work -- large intermediate field of view) *  Keep these progressives and get single-vision computer glasses *  Have these progressives re-made into bifocals and get one of the above computer glasses choices. * Scrap multi-focal lenses entirely and just get an all-purpose intermediate lens (one pair fits al) or one intermediate lens for computer + one distance pair for driving. I don't mind switching between two pair of glasses, but cost is a big factor.  I have an excellent vision plan, and still my portion out of pocket for these progressives was close to $700!!!!  So any computer glasses that are progressive are going cost me big.  Single-vision might cut a couple hundred bucks off, but I'd still be looking at another $400-500 out of pocket even with the computer glasses benefit.  It's always been expensive for me -- I have a whopper of prescription. Given that Pottery Barn has benefited from payment for the product since November 15, 2022 and I made this purchase with the representation by pottery barn that I would have the furniture by Christmas, I was obviously extremely upset by this news. I asked for them to escalate the situation and get back to me immediately. On January 12 at 6 PM when I had not heard anything from Pottery Barn I called again to inquire on the status. main_question: {"author_id": "bonsai-citrus_and_indoor_gardening", "author_name": "bonsai_citrus_and_indoor_gardening", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bonsai-citrus_and_indoor_gardening", "date": "2023-01-28", "text": "Thought I'd share here for those starting out, or for those interested, the repot of a 3.5 ft fukushu kumquat grown indoors year round. I believe this tree was 2-3 years old when I got it and fruiting at the time. It's a grafted tree. It is now 6 years old and outgrew the pot last year. As I was unable to find a new pot (I needed the full size 14 inch pot that matched it's \"twin\" a Nagami kumquat that lives on the other side of tbe window). I refreshed the soil and waited until this year to repot the tree. I believe that due to stress from being rootbound the tree didn't fruit last year. I have these big trees on steel rolling drip trays rated for 500lbs, so to get the tree outside to the repotting area I simply rolled it to the door then lifted it and carried it the 4ft to the edge of my repotting space. I use a cheap painters drop cloth and weigh it down with the soil bags and rocks so that cleanup will be easy, and I can keep pests from outside mostly out of the tree while I repot. The tree was fairly rootbound so it came out of the pot easily. You can see the root mass in the photo below. I had already pulled some of the roots loose before thinking to take a photo.   I should note that I grow in 100% organic soil made from bark, forest products, pumice, sand, some various fertilizers (chicken, bat, feather meal), and both dolomite and oyster shell limes. I use this soil because it is what I might make myself if I had the space to store soil, and it works well as a free draining soil. I also only use organic citrus fertilizers innoculated with mycorrhizae to help break it down in containers. Here is the plant after I worked some of the old soil from the roots. You can see how big the root system is on this tree. (This is a huge contrast to my Nagami, which came from a local greenhouse and had no end to problems. It's root system was probably a quarter the size). It was very healthy. I do use a root rake meant for bonsai trees to loosen the roots and work the soil loose.   Final photo is the tree in its new pot and back in its growing space. I do replace most of the old growing media and plant into new soil every repot. But I also go 3-5 years between repots if I can afford to do so. Since the pot was slightly oversized for the tree I didn't fill it all the way and left two inches at the top. This also helps with watering indoors and minimizes spills. main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-925329097", "author_name": "HU-925329097", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-925329097", "date": "2023-01-29", "text": "Can a home builder with hold keys if we cant agree on final draw. ?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "bry911", "author_name": "bry911", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bry911", "date": "2023-01-29", "text": "@HU-925329097 - I think you need to consult with an attorney before you do anything else.  Whoever produced the buildable plans had a duty to ensure that all measurements were correct, rarely would a builder have a duty to verify measurements on plans that they didn't produce.  If there were contradictory numbers you might argue that they should have sought clarification, but their counter is going to be they had no duty to verify and therefore it wasn't their job to catch the error. In my experience the builder is going to win this and your best bet is to try to negotiate a lower amount.  Of course, I am making a lot of assumptions on the details I don't have and your particular situation may have nuance that will change that. --- In every state it was always your property, even if you haven't paid the builder a single cent.  A builder may have a clause that doesn't allow the owner access to the home during construction, that still doesn't give them the right to keep you out, it just means that your entry on the property would be a breach of contract, I doubt that many courts would find that a material breach, but it is possible. However, the builder's biggest tool to encourage payment is a mechanic's lien.  Mechanic's liens are very easy to get, but harder to perfect.  In other words, there is a good chance that you are going to get a lien on your property even if you don't believe you owe the money.  The builder then has some period of time to perfect the lien.  Perfecting a mechanic's lien is not easy and it can be quite expensive, but if/when perfected your home is in foreclosure, which most people just pay rather than have their home foreclosed on. Again, consult with an attorney in your area, who has construction experience.  I suspect you might be better off paying the contractor and suing him for breach of contract for the driveway than allowing him to get a mechanic's lien.", "images": []}}

title: handicap bathroom design | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "erfriedman14", "author_name": "erfriedman14", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/erfriedman14", "date": "2023-01-29", "text": "Any tips for creating a new bathroom for someone I a wheelchair", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "nancyinmich", "author_name": "Nancy in Mich", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/nancyinmich", "date": "2023-01-29", "text": "Sure!  But be cautious about \u201dUniversal Design.\u201d  I have found that it compromises, trying to be good for all.  Instead, it is good for some and leaves others stranded in a handicapped bathroom on a toilet too far from any wall to get a grip on anything to help you get up!  (Yes, that is my own personal story and I ended up having to turn halfway round and use the plumbing pipes on a flush-o-matic to push off of for a lift, while the stadium usher who took me there was likely wondering if I had drowned!) Universal design works (most of the time) in public facilities, where people of various abilities will be using the bathrooms.  When designing a bathroom for an individual, though, you have the opportunity to meet their own current needs and plan for future changes.  So, your person uses a wheelchair.  Figure out some of their needs by assessing their abilities, need (and future need) for assistance, and the size and plumbing constraints of the room.  Explore technology that can help, like hoyer-type lifts to elaborate ceiling track systems that can pick someone out of their bed or chair into a sling system, then using ceiling tracks, transport them to a commode, bathtub bathtub, or shower in their bathroom.  I have seen a few houses for sale where such track systems were in place, presumably for long-term disabilities. If your person can transfer from their chair to the toilet unaided, you figure out what room they need from which angle, and where grab bars are needed. There are trombone slide like grab bars that mount onto the wall behind the toilet and hinge up agaist the wall or down next to the toilet as needed.  If a person needs somone on one side or other, or beside/behind the toilet to assist, you need to provide room for this.  One wheelchair universal design guideline for commercial spaces said that a handicapped toilet was to have 5 ft of open space on three sides, which is how I, a walker user with bad knees, almost got stranded.  So figure out what is needed now, and what is reasonably to be expected in the future.  If your person needs grab bars, figure where to attach them. Wheelchair accessible sinks are available that hang on a wall or sit on a floating counter that are deep enough to allow a person in a wheelchair pull up and reach the sink without hitting their legs on the wall behind.  Most major manufacturershave one or two.  There are even vanities available that have a bit of storage that will hold these sinks.  They are wall-hung, to allow footrests to swing under the counters without obstruction.  They cost a few thousand dollars, more than they look like they should, presumably due to low consumer need.  Then there are the white plastic pumbing covers that you often see in medical settings below the sinks.  These are installed so that if a user is pulled up under the sink and their leg makes contact with the plumbing, a hot tap water supply pipe or a hot drain won\u2019t burn them. Wheelchair users sometimes use a specially designed shower chair that they transfer into outside the shower (or even in the bedroom) that can be wheeled into a shower and which allows access for reaching to wash most places.  Others, who have good sitting balance, may use a simpler shower stool that they transfer to from the wheelchair.  This would require a more open space and room for the wheelchair to sit in the room while the person is in the shower.  There are also swivel transfer benches that are great for people who can stand to transfer.  They are perhaps 3 ft long and have a chair that swivels and slides along a track.  We used one of these for my father in law before we remodeled our bathroom.  He would stand and pivot so that his back was to the tub, then sit onto the bench seat.  His caregiver would then push the seat backwards while lifting his legs, lock the slider, unlock the swivel, and turn the seat so he was facing the shower controls and lower his legs into the bathtub.  The seat had a back to it and optional arms. For an open showeer situation, where the bather may need assistance at times, there are short, 3 ft tall folding caregiver shower doors.  These keep the water confined into the shower better than a curtain, letting the caregiver stand outside the shower and keep their legs out of the spray.  You top these plastic or glass panel folding shower caregiver doors with a short shower curtain above them that is long enough to stay behid the caregiver doors when the person does not need assistance and is using the sprayer.  Generally, people find it easier to use a chair or stool that is mobile than a built-in shower bench.  It is a matter of being able to reach better to assist a person who is not up against two walls. Think also about whether the wheelchair user might sometimes use a scooter or a power chair.  These may limit how close a person can get to a sink to wash their hands, so a semi-recessed  sink like mine, which protrudes from the counter may be better for them.  These are not necessarily made for handicap use, but  may work better in some circumstances. For the shower itself, you can have a custom tiled shower made to your specifications.  Often, people will use a floor that slopes from the room floor to the back wall of the shower with a long linear drain or trench drain at the back wall.  You will need to consult with a builder or other professional to learn if this is an option for the home.  Constraints sometimes arise about how to fit in the slope needed.  I chose a premade solid surface shower instead.  My drain is at the front of the shower floor, a 4\u201d square you can see in the center front.  It has a half-inch high dam that directs water to remain in the shower and head for the drain and a half-inch deep trough under the metal drain cover.  This is inadequate to hold the water in at times (I went through some hair loss in which I could slow the drain with hair before a single shower was through!) and I do overflow into the bathroom fairly often. main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-778230132", "author_name": "Mac Mac", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-778230132", "date": "2023-01-29", "text": "Hello, Living in a cape cod style home in the New England area. From outside I removed some of the soffit vents and could not see much so stuck up my Iphone and also felt up to the bay and could feel the batts and baffle. From the attic there are baffles in most bays but not all of them and I am not sure if that is because of the dormers(2). title: To Remodel or Not - Is the cost justified? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "svanflicka", "author_name": "svanflicka", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/svanflicka", "date": "2023-01-30", "text": "Hello everyone,I would love to hear your thoughts/opinions about whether the cost of an update/remodel is justified. Specifically, we are living in a 15-year old custom home.  We'll be retiring within 10 years; however our 21-year old son is on the autism spectrum and lives with us.  We're not sure if we will eventually relocate but it's a possibility between 7 - 12 years from now.  We hope our son will be functioning independently at someday. Anyway, our main level of our two-story house is becoming a bit of a time capsule because we haven't updated since we built the house.  The kitchen is red with antique cream cabinetry and a black island while the living room is a mustard yellow and carpeted. I really want a more timeless style.  We are working with a designer and the proposed project is stunning. The remodel will include repainting the cabinets a lighter brighter shade of white (without antiquing), new hardware, new neutral, pale painted walls, quartz to replace the laminate countertops and existing island quartz that won't work with the new color scheme, and a new sink/faucets. Appliances will be replaced with stainless steel in the mid-price range.  We'll install a stained wood range hood to match the medium brown hardwood flooring.  The backsplash will be updated.  The lighting over the island and dining table will be updated too.  We want to bring the medium brown hardwood flooring from the kitchen into the living room to replace the carpet and update the face of the fireplace with a whitewash, over-mortaring, and a beefier mantel to match the flooring.  The living room will be repainted.  One very long wall in the living room will be wainscoted 2/3 of the way up. So this update doesn't include gutting anything or new cabinetry but will still be costly enough. Just wondering if this is worthwhile relative to the cost, as it's expensive. I would appreciate your thoughts. Thanks!", "images": []}

title: Question on load bearing. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "brandon-ring35", "author_name": "Brandon Ring", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/brandon-ring35", "date": "2023-01-30", "text": "First time homeowner. I can do a bit of everything and I'm doing a full renovation.This house has a wall between the living and dining room that bears the floor joists for the second level above. These joists run perpendicular to the first floor joists.I want to remove the wall and replace it with a flush LVL beam. I've designed and calculated the beam and everything looks good. I drilled a small hole down through the subfloor to locate where the support for this wall comes from. It sits right between floor joists with no real support nearby. It seems the entire wall holding the second level joists in this area wasn't properly supported. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mamiller040256", "author_name": "M Miller", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mamiller040256", "date": "2023-01-31", "text": "\"I think they applied the sealer incorrectly.\" It may have not needed sealer at all.  If the stone is too dense to absorb the sealant - as most black granites are - the sealant sits on top of the stone, forming a haze.  This is particularly noticeable if a dish or something is pulled across the counter, streaking the sealant.  There are many granites that do not ever need to be sealed because they are too dense, but unfortunately, many fabricators apply sealant habitually, whether the granite needs it or not. The sealant can be removed with acetone.  If you have some nail polish remover in the house, you can try that, since nail polish remover is acetone.  Otherwise you can get acetone at Home Depot or hardware stores.  A little goes a long way.  It would be best to test an inconspicuous spot with the acetone, and wipe off, and see what happens.  I say inconspicuos spot because there are some black granites being sold that have been dyed to be more black than they originally were.  If that is the case with yours, then the acetone will take off the hazy sealant but also some of the black dye, so test in an inconspicuous spot.", "images": []}}

title: Rose Garden Mulch for tropical south - compost as mulch? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-43509494", "author_name": "Kimberly Wendt (Florida Z. 10b)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-43509494", "date": "2023-01-31", "text": "Was searching the discussions just now, looking for advice on what to use for mulch in my Zone 10b, termite-land South Florida rose garden. Came across a reference to \"Compost IS mulch\" and could be used as mulch. Um, what? When I get compost (either from my own composter bin or in a bag from a store) to me it looks like dirt. Sure it's kinda chunky, but it's dirt. So to my mind, using compost as mulch means actually, you're not mulching your roses. 1. Every known advice says to mulch roses to keep the roots cool, conserve water. What am I missing here? My husband has requested I don't use mulch in the yard for fear of subterranean termites. What should I do? Advice? (None of my rose beds are against the house, but there are two shady beds near the front concrete slab porch. I have put in an 18\" wide and 2\"-3\" deep buffer zone of rock (for drainage and to discourage termites). It will run the entire length of the front concrete slab porch.)", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jacqueline9ca", "author_name": "jacqueline9CA", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jacqueline9ca", "date": "2023-02-01", "text": "I have a comment about weed seeds, or any unwanted seeds. I use a product called Preen, but there are others - they prevent the germination of seeds, but do NOT hurt plants already growing. So, obviously not something you use if you are hoping nearby plants will self seed. However, I have used it forever, and it works fantastically. I only mulch my roses once a year (right after pruning or trimming them, whenever that happens - in a warm climate I can do that most anytime). First I deal with the pruning or trimming, and remove any weeds or nearby ivy or bulbs which have crept too close to the base of the rose. Then, I water the rose well. Then, I sprinkle a handful or two of Osmocote on the soil under the rose out to the drip line of the rose (my theory is that this will provide nitrogen while the compost is  decomposing further, and both of them will feed the rose). Then, I put a layer of at least 3 inches of home made compost my DH makes on top of the soil out to the drip line, of course keeping at least 3-4 inches away from the base of the rose. Then I sprinkle Preen or some similar product all over the top of the compost, and (very important) water it in. Voila - done for the year. By the time a year has gone by, the compost has fed the rose and turned into soil, so I repeat the process. I also use Preen on bare soil if, say, an area has just been weeded and is all clean. It has worked like a charm always, and although nothing is 100%, it reduces the amount of new weeds by certainly 95%. Regarding my DH's compost. Our property is a city lot of only 1/3rd of an acre, but we have a lot of mature trees, most of which are deciduous. He makes it from grass clippings and shredded leaves (the small leaves don't need to be shredded - just the large oak leaves) from the trees in a very large sort of raised bed place he built in the back of the lot, which he can leave open to the rain, or cover with a thick plastic sheet to let the compost rot and get hot underneath. Then when the Fall cleanup has produce MORE leaves, etc, he bags up last years crop which has sat for 12 months already, and puts it in those huge strong black garbage bags - it usually makes 7-8 of them. It stays in those bags until eventually one by one the bags are  dumped into a medium sized plastic garbage can which lives on my wheeled garden trolly, so it is easy to wheel it to where I am working in the garden. One crop lasts me about 12 months. So, there is always one bagged crop aging further, and one new crop in the compost raised bed, while the trees grow another crop of leaves... I like it because, after sitting for 12-24 months it is the darkest, most wonderful compost, and the roses love it. Also free - what's not to like? Jackie", "images": []}}

Out west, our water and soils are usually highly salty and mineralized. Much of our soil is clay/adobe with limited drainage and very little (historically) rain so the \"salty\" water doesn't get flushed through the salty soil very well and it is increasingly causing issues.
